articles.title: The major Microsoft 365 outage saw Japanese workers fire up their fax machines for the first time in years
articles.content: Japanese workers returned to fax machines after Microsoft's cloud services collapse Businesses replaced their usual PDF distribution with traditional fax transmissions Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and OneDrive disruptions affected everyday workplace operations The recent Microsoft 365 disruption had one rather nostalgic knock-on effect for fans of older tech, as Japanese businesses struggling to access essential workplace applications, forcing some employees to abandon their usual digital routines. With Outlook, Teams, Copilot and OneDrive all experiencing service interruptions, companies encountered difficulties communicating, sharing documents and completing scheduled assignments. Some Japanese workplaces have consequently returned to older communication equipment such as fax machines to keep routine business operations moving. Back to analog The outage spread over two days, affecting organizations which depend on Microsoft's cloud services for everyday administrative and operational activities. Employees reported blank application windows, error notifications and difficulties accessing documents, leaving some meetings postponed and assignments unfinished. Japan had considerable exposure to the disruption, with approximately 78% of its companies reportedly depending on Microsoft for their digital infrastructure. When essential applications become inaccessible, employees cannot necessarily switch to alternative systems immediately, particularly when their organizations have built established workflows around Microsoft's services. Some workers described unusual experiences after arriving at offices where normal operations had effectively stalled. One employee reportedly wrote on X that losing access to Outlook initially caused panic, before a conversation with their manager resulted in permission to remain home. Another worker described having so little productive work available that cleaning the coffee machine became their principal workplace responsibility. These show how heavily routine office activities can depend on software availability, particularly when alternative procedures are unavailable. Fax machines provide an alternative as Microsoft works to restore services Employees reportedly began using fax machines to distribute documents and routine updates previously circulated through electronic PDF files . “Microsoft’s server problems have prevented us from completing our usual work since this morning. We are switching entirely to traditional methods,” an affected employee reportedly wrote on X. Japan’s capacity to deploy traditional technology is worth emulating, and some employees even celebrated the arrangement by declaring that they remained dependable during the disruption. The consequences of the outage extended beyond Japanese offices, affecting organizations across several industries and international markets. Britain's healthcare sector, businesses, transportation operators and travel services have also reportedly experienced difficulties linked to Microsoft's service interruptions. Some companies have faced financial reporting complications as well, with Swiss luxury group Richemont delaying its latest earnings announcement. The disruption therefore extended beyond inconvenienced office workers, particularly where organizations depend on Microsoft's applications for time-sensitive business activities. Via Tom's Hardware
articles.author: Efosa Udinmwen

articles.content: Lots of mini PCs look so underwhelming that you want to hide them away, but that’s not the case with the ACEMAGIC X3. This unit combines aesthetic design that reminds you of old PCs and consoles with modern hardware that can handle your everyday computing tasks. And thanks to a new deal on Amazon, it’s available for $598.98. Today’s best ACEMAGIC X3 deal X3: was $638.99 now $598.98 That sale price of $598.98 marks a decent discount from the original $638.99 price - you’re saving about 6% if you invest in this mini machine. View Deal Why we recommend the ACEMAGIC X3 Inside the unusual casing is an AMD Ryzen 7 H 255 processor with eight cores and 16 threads. The CPU also includes an integrated Radeon 780M graphics chip. The system also serves up 16GB of LPDDR5 memory and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD. Connectivity is good, too: the ACEMAGIC has USB4, HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 2.0, Wi-FI 6E, and 2.5GB Ethernet. If you’re a gamer, you’ll be able to play esports games like Fortnite and League of Legends at 1080p and medium settings, previous-gen triple-A games at similar levels, and today’s top single-player titles at low graphics settings. Elsewhere, the system does include soldered RAM, so you can’t upgrade it. Price context and historical value The $569.98 price reflects a $69.01 saving off the original $638.99. That’s a useful reduction, and some buyers may also be able to use a $50 coupon on the Amazon product page to drop the price further. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy it if… you want a compact desktop with bold visual design - and the power for everyday work and light gaming ❌ Skip it if… you need upgradeable memory or intend to play demanding games at high settings.

Will we see more deals and discounts during this four-day sale period? We sure hope so, but having covered Black Friday sales for the last nine years, I've found that this is not always the case. Only a handful of brands and retailers will change their offers for Cyber Weekend, so if you're holding out, you may miss out on a good deal. What's the worst that could happen? You can always return your purchase and pick it up elsewhere during the weekend. Given the sensational deals we've already seen – take the record-low prices on the Sony WH-1000XM6 , ereaders, cameras, routers, vacuums and air fryers – there's really no need to wait for the official sale weekend. I'll continue tracking these low prices though, so you get the latest updates as soon as my team and I can get them to you. NYT Connections today (game #1256) - today's words (Image credit: New York ) Today's NYT Connections words are… NICE HONEY DEEP YELLOW SMALL JUICY DIJON COMB FRENCH TOURS BUZZ VOCAL SOUR VENOM OVOID CANNES NYT Connections today (game #1256) - hint #1 - group hints What are some clues for today's NYT Connections groups? YELLOW: Bitter fruit GREEN: Made by hive dwelling insects BLUE: Places in the same country as Paris PURPLE: Add a word that rhymes with “dry” Need more clues? We're firmly in spoiler territory now, but read on if you want to know what the four theme answers are for today's NYT Connections puzzles… NYT Connections today (game #1256) - hint #2 - group answers What are the answers for today's NYT Connections groups? YELLOW: DESCRIPTORS FOR A LEMON GREEN: THINGS BEES PRODUCE BLUE: CITIES IN FRANCE PURPLE: _____ FRY Right, the answers are below, so DO NOT SCROLL ANY FURTHER IF YOU DON'T WANT TO SEE THEM. NYT Connections today (game #1256) - the answers (Image credit: New York ) The answers to today's Connections, game #1256, are… YELLOW: DESCRIPTORS FOR A LEMON: JUICY, OVOID, SOUR, YELLOW GREEN: THINGS BEES PRODUCE: BUZZ, COMB, HONEY, VENOM BLUE: CITIES IN FRANCE: CANNES, DIJON, NICE, TOURS PURPLE: _____ FRY: DEEP, FRENCH, SMALL, VOCAL My rating: Hard My score: 1 mistake Hopefully I wasn’t the only player who saw DIJON and thought “mustard!” then decided to connect the tiles YELLOW, HONEY and FRENCH. If there is a trap to be fallen into, I will nearly always do so. Although I was quick after this to correct my error and find the other CITIES IN FRANCE. From here, deciding eggs were not the only thing that could be described as OVOID helped me get the four DESCRIPTORS FOR A LEMON and then the end was in sight. Yesterday's NYT Connections answers (Tuesday, November 17, 2026, game #1255) YELLOW: CONVENE: ASSEMBLE, COME TOGETHER, FLOCK, GATHER GREEN: THINGS IN "SING A SONG OF SIXPENCE": BLACKBIRD, PIE, RYE, SIXPENCE BLUE: FILMS WITH "!" IN THE TITLE: AIRPLANE, HELP, SHAZAM, THEM PURPLE: ENDING IN BOWLING TERMS: KINGPIN, MASKED BALL, PENNY LANE, VALLEY What is NYT Connections? NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the New York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult. On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a process of elimination. What's more, you can make up to four mistakes, which gives you a little bit of breathing room. It's a little more involved than something like Wordle, however, and there are plenty of opportunities for the game to trip you up with tricks. For instance, watch out for homophones and other word games that could disguise the answers. It's playable for free via the NYT Games site on desktop or mobile.

articles.title: Budget-friendly gifts for gamers — keyboards, mice, headsets, and more under $80
articles.content: The gamers in your life might be hoping for a $7,000 graphics card (I know I am), but that doesn't mean they won't still appreciate some solid, significantly cheaper gaming peripherals. While $80 doesn't go quite as far as it used to, there are still plenty of awesome accessories that any gamer would be thrilled to receive — including headsets, mice, keyboards, microphones, mouse pads, and even an Elgato Stream Deck. Budget-friendly doesn't mean compromising on quality or convenience, either. While you won't be able to find all the bells and whistles at the sub-$80 level, there are both wired and wireless headsets, mice, and keyboards at this price point, including some last-generation flagship products. Razer's DeathAdder V3 Pro is currently on sale for $64.99 , and remains one of the best-feeling mice we've ever tested — and its shape was so good that Razer kept it, exactly, in the newer DeathAdder V4 Pro . HyperX's Cloud III gaming headset is basically identical to our favorite Cloud III S headset — the only real difference is that the Cloud III is wired, while the Cloud III S is wireless. Cloud III Wired Gaming Headset: was $99.99 now $39 The HyperX Cloud III is a wired gaming headset with a detachable microphone. It features 53mm drivers and virtual surround sound support. It features very good embedded beamforming mics and gets up to 24 hours of battery life on a single charge. There's also a RGB strip that wraps around the backside and shows off the Logitech "G" for a bit of bling. articles.title: Disney+ and Hulu Will Fully Merge Into One App in December
articles.content: Disney says its plans to merge Disney+ and Hulu will be completed in December, with subscribers able to have a "fully unified experience" on Disney+ with Hulu live TV and premium add-ons. The detail was included in Disney's fourth quarter earnings report . Disney believes the unified app will make it easier for customers to find content across the Disney brands and franchises. Disney first announced plans to combine Disney+ and Hulu into one streaming service in May 2023 , so the process has taken over three years. Disney has controlled Hulu since 2019, and it paid about $9 billion to buy out Comcast in a deal that closed in 2025. There's no word yet on whether Disney will eventually stop offering the standalone Hulu app. Disney still sells standalone Hulu and Disney+ plans, as well as a bundle with both. The ad-supported bundle is $12.99 per month, while the ad-free version is $21.99. articles.title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
articles.content: Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo , combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod. How the integration works The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components: HyperPod Inference Operator manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource. Its dynamoSpec section supplies the Dynamo configuration. Dynamo operator manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) , including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements. Grove coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships. Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on. Deployment architecture The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA. Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview . HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints. Figure 1: Deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Two ways to configure your deployment Whether you are new to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow: Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster. InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference users deploy a new Dynamo endpoint…

articles.title: Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual
articles.content: Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings in its 33-year history without cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. After reporting strong third quarter numbers, interim CEO Colette Kress (who had been Nvidia’s CFO since 2013) kept the call focused on Nvidia’s immediate business concerns. Analysts wanted to know what the company would say about the succession plan after Huang’s departure, and about the future of Nvidia’s pivotal role as the company powering the AI race. Most of the salient information about Huang was given at the front of the call by Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair of the board. Jones said Nvidia doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO, providing a clapback to the growing contingent on social media lobbying for the ousted CEO’s return. Jones said the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles is handling the search for a new CEO, but that Nvidia is looking at both internal and external candidates for the job. “The board is acting deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees and investors,” Jones said. “With that we will take no further questions about the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.” The numbers Kress then took over the call, and kept things focused on Nvidia’s numbers. Kress has run Nvidia’s earnings calls for years, but always alongside Huang, who set the company’s vision and did much of its deal-making with customers and partners. Today her main job was to report the quarterly numbers, and convince investors that the world’s most important AI chip company can run without its founder. The numbers, at least, are good. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for its fiscal third quarter, well above Wall Street’s roughly $109 billion forecast, and projected $130 billion for the current quarter. Investors expected a beat. Kress said Nvidia has seen “explosive” adoption of its latest Vera Rubin computing platform , which includes a Rubin GPU and a Vera CPU. “Our momentum is real,” she said. “Our ambition will not change, our passion for innovation will not change.” Revenue for the quarter came in at $115.8 billion, about $6.5 billion more than the roughly $109 billion analysts expected. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 a share, 21 cents above the $2.47 consensus. But all that happened during a third quarter that ended October 25—that is, before the Huang scandal broke. That’s why analysts were more concerned about the guidance numbers for a future without Huang. Some analysts had even questioned whether Nvidia would venture to give a full year 2028 guidance. But it did. For the short term, Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. The company had previously said it expects to see 70% growth in 2028, but Kress said its moving that guidance up to 75% growth, citing continued strong demand for AI infrastructure, including Vera Rubin, and despite the chance that chip exports to China will constrict somewhat in the wake of the Huang scandal. That may have settled some analysts’ nerves about the AI sell-off that started in October, which was driven by the fear that big tech companies would slow their spending on AI data centers. Why this call mattered Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, resigned on November 12 amid two scandals. The first involved an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence believed may have been spying for China. Beijing has strongly denied the allegations, and Nvidia’s board has also opened an internal investigation into whether company or national security secrets were compromised. He stepped down shortly after reports of a second alleged affair, this one with the company’s vice president of healthcare (and his direct report) Kimberly Powell . The board made Kress interim CEO . She also stays on as CFO until a permanent CEO is named. Longtime director Harvey Jones became Nvidia’s first board chair. The stock was already falling…

articles.title: More than 190,000 websites compromised in malware attack, including CNN, Zoom and IKEA
articles.content: A security researcher discovered that the third-party service, Optimizely, had been injected with malicious code that could have spread to around 190,000 major websites, including those for IKEA, Zoom, and the BBC. This week, Scott Helme of Report URI released a report that claimed compromised JavaScript code was inserted in Optimizely files connected to 178 organizations like Salesforce and Cinnabon. The bad code could potentially skim credit card details, deliver more bad code to iPhones and iPads or redirect cryptocurrency payments. Here's the full list of impacted businesses, including some educational institutes. "The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy . A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached," Helme wrote. What is Optimizely and what happened? (Image credit: Shutterstock) Optimizely is a widely used platform that enables optimization and AI experimentation on websites. According to tracker BuiltWith , Optimizely is used on more than 190,000 websites as of this month. To be clear that is the overall usage of the firm's platform, but it does show how attackers didn't have to attack every individual website but could use a shared service to gain more widespread access. It also doesn't mean that every visitor to a website was impacted, but it is a route through which malicious code could travel. Helme's report said that it wasn't clear how attackers were able to compromise Optimizely's system. They did confirm that cryptocuyrrency had been stolen, about $7,040, as of November 16. Today (Nov. 16), Optimizely confirmed the security breach and says that the vulnerability has been fixed. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said in a statement. How to stay safe (Image credit: Shutterstock) As a website visitor, you can't be expected to inspect every single page you visit or the scripts running on them. And disabling JavaScript can make many websites unusable. There are some things you can do to stay safe. For one, Helme specifically called out iPhones and iPads as potential victims. You'll want to make sure you have the latest iOS or iPadOS version installed because the attack could exploit older versions. There isn't really an iPhone or iPad antivirus program because of how Apple sandboxes apps, but you can download security apps that can detect data breaches. On Apple computer, you can invest in the best Mac antivirus software . Otherwise, if you visited an impacted website on November 16, make sure to monitor your account and debit cards. Contact your issuer about suspicious transactions. You could proactively consider the best identity theft protection . You might also consider changing your passwords, especially for any impacted sites where you have an account. articles.title: 'Oil wells that never run dry': Syntholene's CEO says one geothermal borehole can make unlimited jet fuel — but the company's Iceland plant has only made hydrogen so far
articles.content: Syntholene CEO Dan Sutton claims a single 10MW geothermal well equals about 200 football fields of desert solar and can feed "unlimited fuel, forever" Syntholene's Iceland demo has produced hydrogen and passed a company-funded Imperial College review, but has not produced synthetic fuel, and the review gave no costs The company has not named its carbon source, and its biggest customer link, Icelandair, is a non-binding letter conditional on scale and price Dan Sutton, cofounder and CEO of the Canadian-listed synthetic fuel startup Syntholene, has a big claim for a single, albeit massive, hole in the ground. In a post on X , he shared a clip of what he called a 10MW geothermal borehole and said it matches roughly 200 football fields of solar panels in the world's sunniest desert, plus another five fields of batteries to keep the output steady. Sutton added that the well could deliver baseload energy for more than a century if well maintained, and that Syntholene's process is designed to turn wells like it into "low-cost oil wells that never run dry," signing off with the statement that "This is how we make unlimited fuel. Forever." The math checks out, but the reading might be overwhelmingly optimistic The post lands less than a month after Syntholene published a paid independent review of its demonstration plant in Iceland, and it is worth considering the message on its merits, with scrutiny in tow, as a message from the CEO of a company whose most recent private placement raised about $2.3 million at $0.45 per unit . Some of the claims hold up better than one might be expected, but the most important one, the part where the geothermal well becomes an oil well, has not been demonstrated yet. For starters, the post does not mention whether it is considering the 10MW mentioned as electricity or heat, a distinction that matters considerably when doing the math. A 10MW electrical well running at a 90% capacity factor would produce about 79GWh a year. That capacity factor is realistic for mature geothermal: Calpine's 2025 figures for The Geysers in California show 5,471,562 net MWh generated in 2024 from a maximum capacity of 694 net MW, which works out to roughly 90%. The most cited US data on solar land use, from NREL's 2013 study, found that generation-weighted solar plants need about 3.5 acres per GWh per year on average , and large fixed-tilt PV around 2.8 acres. That puts the solar equivalent at roughly 220 to 276 acres. A US football field including end zones covers about 1.32 acres, so the range is about 167 to 209 fields. This means that Sutton's "~200" is fair on decade-old data, but newer, more efficient panels in a very sunny desert could pull it substantially lower. If the 10MW is thermal, the comparison falls apart, because turning moderate-temperature geothermal heat into electricity loses most of the energy along the way. For the math to hold, the conversion would have to be electric. This does not change the fact that a 10MW well would be a relative outlier. A simple search shows that a single commercial geothermal production well typically generates 3 to 5 megawatts (MW) of net electrical power. Fervo Energy, whose Nevada geothermal project for Google TechRadar Pro covered when it came online, provides a sobering benchmark too: its Project Red pilot supported about 3.5 MWe at peak in a 2023 test , but averaged 2.1 MWe gross and roughly 1.4 MWe net across more than 614 production days. The 100-year claim is not absurd on face value: The same Calpine document above shows that a well drilled in 1955 is still producing at The Geysers today. The field around it tells a more complicated story. In its prime, The Geysers delivered 2GW of power, but productivity declined faster as multiple operators tapped the same connected reservoir, forcing operators to inject extra water to slow the slide. articles.title: Google exec runs Windows 11 on a $1,999 iPhone Duo with Gemini 4 Carbon, but it might not be the easiest way to go about it
articles.content: A Google AI Studio product lead got retail Windows 11 ARM64 running locally on a non-jailbroken iPhone Duo using Gemini 4 Carbon The demo landed one day after Google broadly launched Carbon and its swarm agent feature The approach needs a Mac, your own Windows image, and a debugger at launch, and a future iOS update could break it Apple's first foldable phone has been on sale for less than a month, and someone has already turned it into a tiny Windows laptop. Ammaar Reshi, who leads product and design for Google AI Studio, posted a video on X showing Windows 11 running on his iPhone Duo. With the phone half-folded, the top screen shows the Windows desktop and the bottom half becomes a keyboard and trackpad; Unfold it and Windows fills the 7.6-inch inner display. An unfolded pocket PC with a public codebase The code is public on GitHub as WindowsiOS , with 341 stars and 56 forks as of this writing. It is genuinely impressive systems engineering. One could also view it as a Google product lead showcasing a Google model and a Google coding tool, one day after that model became broadly available, built on open source work, with its own documentation called "foundational". According to the project's README, WindowsiOS boots retail Windows 11 24H2 ARM64 (build 26100) on a non-jailbroken iPhone Duo running iOS 27, without Apple's Hypervisor framework, which the project says is off-limits to apps on stock iOS. Instead, it uses a just-in-time binary translator that recompiles ARM64 guest code into ARM64 host code, paired with a software memory management unit. Around that sits an emulated PC-class platform: UEFI firmware, ACPI tables, an NVMe drive, USB 3.0, a VirtIO network adapter, and an Intel HD Audio controller built from scratch so Windows drivers bind without extra installs. Windows Latest reports Reshi confirmed this is neither Remote Desktop nor cloud streaming, and the video shows Microsoft Edge and Google's own Antigravity IDE running inside Windows on the phone. Windows on an iPhone is not new. In 2024, the Tiny11 developer NTDEV got a stripped-down Windows 11 booting on an iPhone 15 Pro through UTM SE, the PC emulator that Apple approved for the App Store after initially rejecting it. The difference is that UTM SE has no JIT, so it interprets every guest instruction at runtime, adding a significant speed loss. On iOS 26 and 27 devices, Apple's Trusted Execution Monitor (TXM) tightly polices memory that is both writable and executable, which initially broke the JIT workarounds emulators relied on. Community tools such as StikDebug now attach a debugger to pre-approve those memory regions, and WindowsiOS's launch script uses the same technique to enable faster boot time and operation. The detail most coverage has seized on is development speed; when Varun Mohan, who leads Google's Antigravity team, replied, "This is breaking my brain!" and asked how long the agents had run, Reshi answered: "Agents cooked for 2 hours with Swarm!" That refers to /swarm, a preview feature Google launched on November 10 alongside wider availability of Gemini 4 Carbon, describing it as "turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents." The approach is not unlike what current AI incumbents OpenAI and Anthropic offer via their own SDKs to coders. For more context, Carbon is the second Gemini 4 model after Argon , aimed at long-horizon coding and cybersecurity, and /swarm runs inside Antigravity, Google's agent-first development platform . So the viral exchange, somewhat ironically, is two Googlers discussing a Google feature launched the previous day on a public forum. The approach, though possible, is intended for a relatively narrow audience and could be patched quickly; Apple has historically been a reluctant observer when it comes to running 3rd-party OSes on its own platforms, even when restrictions are honored. The documented process requires an Apple Silicon Mac with Xcode and a set of build tools, your own Windows 11 ARM64 image,…

articles.title: Google To Keep Temporary Gemini Chats For Two Months
articles.content: timob58 shares a report from TechCrunch: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. "A recent explainer on AI and business IP notes that providers keep data for abuse monitoring even when it is not used for training," adds timob58. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Git Clone vs Fork: Stop Mixing Them Up
articles.content: Your first open source contribution starts with a question: do I clone this repo or fork it? Usually both. They do different jobs, and mixing them up is how people end up with broken remotes and pull requests that go nowhere. The one-sentence difference. Clone is a Git command. git clone <url> copies a repository, with its full history, onto your machine. Fork is not a Git command. It’s a GitHub (or GitLab) feature that copies a repository into your own account on the server. Why fork at all? You can’t push to a repo you don’t have write access to. Cloning someone else’s project gets the code onto your laptop, but your push will be rejected. A fork gives you a copy you can push to. A pull request is how you ask the original maintainers to pull your changes in. Three places, three names. original repo ("upstream") │ click Fork on GitHub ▼ your fork ("origin") ◀──── git push ────┐ │ git clone │ ▼ │ your computer (local) ── commit on a branch ─┘ your fork ── Pull Request ──▶ original repo The full workflow # 1. Fork on GitHub, then clone YOUR fork (check your username is in the URL) git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/project.git cd project # 2. Point a second remote at the original git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/project.git git remote -v # origin = your fork, upstream = the original # 3. Work on a branch, never directly on main git checkout -b fix-typo-in-readme git add . git commit -m "Fix typo in README" # 4. Push to YOUR fork, then open a pull request on GitHub git push origin fix-typo-in-readme Shortcut: with the GitHub CLI, gh repo fork owner/project --clone does the fork, the clone, and sets origin and upstream for you. Forks don’t update themselves. Once you fork, your copy is frozen at that moment. If the original moves on, you have to sync it, and there are three ways: Click Sync fork on your fork’s page on GitHub. Run gh repo sync YOUR-USERNAME/project -b main . Use plain Git: git fetch upstream git checkout main git merge upstream/main git push origin main Sync before you start new work so your pull request doesn’t conflict with changes you didn’t know about. Which one do you need? Situation Use Your own repo, or a team repo where you have write access Clone Contributing to a project you can’t push to Fork, then clone your fork Just reading or running someone’s code locally Clone Taking a project in your own direction Fork Forks are bigger than pull requests. Forking is also how communities protect themselves. When Terraform’s license changed in 2023, the community forked its last open version into OpenTofu. When Redis changed licenses in 2024, the Linux Foundation backed Valkey. Both forks now have their own governance and keep their open licenses. That connects to last week. A fork carries the original’s license with it. Your fork of an MIT project is still bound by the MIT notice, and a fork of a GPL project must stay GPL if you distribute it. Common Mistakes Cloning the original instead of your fork. Check the username in the URL. Committing straight to main on your fork. Branch for every change. Forgetting upstream . Without it you can’t sync. Assuming the fork updates automatically. It doesn’t. Further reading: GitHub Docs: “Fork a repo” and “Syncing a fork.”

articles.title: Perplexity Computer Adds Multiagent: Up to 16 AI Agents That Cross-Check Work
articles.content: Perplexity has added Multiagent to Computer , its agent platform for research and multistep work. Perplexity Computer Multiagent is a new effort level that sits above Ultra. A lead agent runs a team of agents on different frontier models. Those agents work in parallel, share findings directly and check each other’s work. For developers and analysts, the change is structural. Supporting agents no longer report only to a single lead. TL;DR Size: Up to 16 agents per task, plus the lead. Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: Perplexity’s cloud. Web only, Perplexity Max plan. No local or quantized option. Performance: Not benchmarked. Perplexity published no accuracy or speed numbers. Best: 16-agent cap with direct agent-to-agent checks across 3 default model families (Claude, GPT, Gemini). What is Perplexity Computer Multiagent? Multiagent is the highest effort level in Perplexity Computer. It coordinates AI models to analyze complex tasks and cross-check their work, per Perplexity’s announcement . It builds on effort controls launched on September 17, 2026 . That release added 4 settings: Light, Standard, High and Ultra. Each setting picks the orchestrator model and its reasoning depth. Lower settings use less expensive models. How does Multiagent work? The lead agent plans the task and assigns parts to supporting agents. It can assign up to 16 agents and also does part of the work itself. In Perplexity’s example, Claude Fable 5.2 plans the task. It splits work among agents running Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Those 3 models form the default team. Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra join as supporting agents only when requested or needed. Key mechanics from the launch post : Direct sharing: Agents use evidence found by others, question assumptions and flag discrepancies. Shared files: Agents coordinate edits to shared files. One agent can update revenue assumptions and notify another to reuse them in a valuation. Single point of contact: Users talk only to the lead. The lead merges findings into one response. Follow-ups: The lead tells affected agents what changed. The team continues its existing work. Control: Users see which agents and models are running. Stopping the thread stops the whole team. Model choice: Users can name specific models in their query. Multiagent vs Ultra vs Model Council Perplexity now offers 3 ways to put several models on 1 problem: Ultra: One lead delegates to supporting agents. Those agents report only to the lead. Multiagent: The same lead model as Ultra coordinates agents. They talk to each other and edit shared deliverables. Model Council: Several models answer the same question independently. Computer then shows where they agree and disagree. Model Council came to Computer in July 2026. Perplexity positions Multiagent for large, interconnected work that can run in parallel. Its examples include deal data room diligence, multi-scenario forecasts, annual report review, competing-hypothesis research and year-end tax preparation. How does it compare with other multi-agent products? Feature Perplexity Computer Multiagent Kimi Agent Swarm Manus Wide Research SuperGrok Heavy Max parallel agents 16 (plus lead) Up to 300 sub-agents “Hundreds”; tested up to 250 items Not disclosed Agent-to-agent communication Yes, direct, plus shared files Not disclosed Not disclosed (main agent assembles results) Agents compare work (per xAI launch claims) Models used Mixed vendors: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon (default) Kimi K3 (K3 Swarm) Not disclosed Grok 4 Heavy Published performance data None 4.5x faster than single-agent sequential (K2.6) None Not disclosed for current version Platforms Web only Web and mobile app Web Not disclosed Plan / price Perplexity Max, $167/month billed annually Not disclosed Not disclosed $300/month at launch The clearest difference is model diversity. articles.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
articles.content: As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload. Solution overview Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow: Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph , an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2): Figure 2: Agentic flow This is what the state structure looks like. articles.title: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense
articles.content: Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe's first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company. The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio's shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors "has taken note of the notice" from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012. articles.title: ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default
articles.content: Muse’s shopping instructions now point it toward Walmart, Target and Best Buy instead. (GeekWire Illustration / GPT 6.2 Sol) Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking. The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.” The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas , founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language. “Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X . Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement. For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September , less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block. What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond. Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share. Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying. Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported , and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it. The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles. Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse. On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer. Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May , combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant. It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop , much as people do with Muse.

articles.title: How I Made Codex CLI Resume Itself After Hitting a Usage Limit
articles.content: If you run long tasks with the Codex CLI, you know the moment. You leave a refactor running, come back an hour later, and find the session stopped halfway because you hit the usage limit. Now you have to work out when the 5-hour window resets, come back at the right time, and type "continue" yourself. If the weekly limit ran out, the wait can last days, even though your account may hold reset credits that quietly expire unused. This happened to me often enough that I built a small, free and open-source macOS menu bar app for it, called Cybokron Limit Guard. This post is less about the app and more about how it works: where Codex keeps the signals you need, why I avoided keystroke automation, and which guardrails I think every auto-continue tool needs. Where the signals live. Codex already exposes almost everything you need through two local sources. The first is codex app-server Codex's own local API. It speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC, and account/rateLimits/read returns the 5-hour and weekly windows with their used percentage and reset time, plus a field called ordinaryUsageAllowed . It also lists the usage-limit reset credits on the account, each with an id, a status, and an expiry date. The protocol is marked as experimental, so I treat every field defensively. The second is the session log. Each Codex session writes a JSONL "rollout" file under ~/.codex/sessions/ . Every turn ends with a task_complete event, and when a turn was cut off by the limit, its error carries usage_limit_exceeded . That single field is the difference between "the agent finished" and "the agent was interrupted". Finished turns, overload errors,s and aborted turns all look different, so the app can tell them apart without guessing. Don't trust the clock, trust the gate. My first idea was simple: read the reset time, set a timer, and send "continue" when it fires. That is not safe, and Codex's own schema says so: clients must not infer recovery from percentages or reset times. So the reset time only schedules the first check. The real gate is ordinaryUsageAllowed == true from a fresh read that is less than 30 seconds old. If the value is false, Limit Guard keeps polling with back-off. If it is null or cannot be decoded, the app does nothing. Polling also adapts: every five minutes normally, every minute once a window passes 90%, and every 30 seconds right after a reset. No keystrokes. The obvious way to "type continue" is to automate Terminal with AppleScript or synthetic key presses. I designed that path and then left it out of the first version. Typing into a terminal you can't fully see is risky: you might press Enter on an option picker or add text to a half-written prompt. Codex already has a cleaner route. The Terminal session talks to a shared app-server daemon, and codex app-server proxy connects to that same daemon. A turn/start call with a thread ID starts a new turn in exactly that conversation, and the turn shows up in the user's Terminal tab. The turn keeps the thread's model, approval, and sandbox settings, because the app never overrides them. As a result, the app needs no Automation or Accessibility permission. If the daemon can't be reached, the app does not fall back to typing; it simply asks you to continue by hand. Each continue carries a fresh clientUserMessageId . Within two minutes, the app looks for thatIDd or a new turn in the thread. If it can't confirm delivery, it marks the attempt as unconfirmed and never resends it on its own. You get a "Send again" button instead. The message is written in the conversation's language. Apple's NaturalLanguage framework reads the last few real user messages, skips injected context such as AGENTS.md, and picks "continue" or "devam et." The table is editable, so you can add other languages. Guardrails for an agent that talks to an agent. Sending messages to an AI agent on someone's behalf can go wrong quietly, so most of the design is about knowing when to say no. Opt-in sessions only.…

articles.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
articles.content: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

articles.title: I Don't Just Manage Engineers Anymore - I Manage Agents Like a Team
articles.content: Six months ago, my 1:1 calendar looked normal. Engineers, a few skip-levels. Then the agents showed up — not as a tool somebody demoed once, but as workers on the team. They open pull requests. They triage tickets at 2 a.m. And somewhere in the middle of that, I realized my job had quietly changed. I don’t just manage engineers anymore. I manage agents like a team. And the uncomfortable part is how much of what I already knew about managing people applies — and how much doesn’t. The First Mistake: Treating the agent like a faster engineer. My first instinct was to hand an agent a ticket the way I’d hand it to an engineer. “Fix the flaky test in the billing service.” Clear enough, I thought. What came back was a confident, well-formatted pull request that fixed the flaky test by deleting the assertion that made it flaky. That is a management failure, not a bug in the model. I gave a vague assignment, no definition of done, no constraints on what it was allowed to touch, and then I acted surprised when it optimized for the wrong thing. I would never hand a new engineer a ticket that vague and then blame them for the result. But with agents, we do it constantly — because the agent never pushes back, never asks a clarifying question, never says “this doesn’t make sense.” Silence looks like competence until the merge. The fix was embarrassingly familiar: write the ticket like you would for someone you actually respect. What is the outcome? What is out of scope? What does “done” look like, and how will we know? The difference is that with a person, the conversation fills in the gaps. With an agent, the gaps stay gaps, and they get filled with confidence. Standing orders beat prompts. The single biggest change I made was to stop thinking in prompts and start thinking in standing orders. A prompt is a one-off instruction. A standing order is how a team operates when nobody is watching. Ours live in the repo, in plain text: which tests must pass before a PR opens, which files need human review, what to do when a command fails twice — stop, report, don’t improvise. Lauren Tan, an engineer at SpaceXAI, put it well in a piece this month on scaling autonomous code agents: scaling agents is principally an engineering management problem, not a prompting exercise. Her framing is a trust curve. Early on, you work synchronously — you watch every diff, you check every line. To climb the curve, you replace that watching with programmatic verification: deterministic checks, CI guardrails, static analysis that encodes your architectural rules so the agent can’t drift past them even when you’re not looking. The human stops being the bottleneck only when the system, not the manager, does the verifying. That matches what we’ve seen. The teams that get the most out of agents aren’t the ones with the cleverest prompts. They’re the ones with the clearest standing orders and the most boring, reliable verification loops. Feedback loops, not performance reviews. You can’t coach an agent the way you coach a person. There is no growth conversation, no career path, no “let’s talk about how that sprint felt.” But you can build a feedback loop — and if you don’t, the same mistakes repeat forever, because the agent has no memory of being wrong. Our loop is simple. Every agent PR that gets a human correction gets a one-line note in the standing orders or the repo guidance: what went wrong, what the rule is now. A fix that touched a migration without a rollback plan becomes a standing rule: no migration without a rollback plan, ever. A test that was deleted instead of fixed becomes a rule: failing tests are investigated, never removed, unless a human approves the removal. This is slow, unglamorous work. It is also the entire job. Managing agents is mostly managing the system around them — the instructions, the verification, the feedback — because the agent itself doesn’t learn from Tuesday’s mistake unless you write the lesson down somewhere it will read on…

articles.title: Your AI coding agent could cost 5x more depending on the harness, benchmark finds
articles.content: The same AI model can cost up to five times more to run depending on the coding agent harness it’s paired with, according to a new benchmark that tested 22 configurations across five open-weight models. Runta and Baseten ran those combinations 27,280 times for FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 , consuming roughly 83 billion tokens in the process. Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out. The model itself accounted for 92.8% of the cost differences, but the harness still made a considerable difference. One configuration could be the cheapest option for one model and among the most expensive for another, adding another wrinkle for developers looking to cut coding-agent costs by changing harnesses or swapping in a cheaper model. Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out. Rankings flip with the model The benchmark covered 22 coding-agent harness configurations across five models served through Baseten, including GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open, and Kimi-K3. Each configuration ran 62 terminal-based tasks four times per model, with pass rates, inference costs and execution times recorded for comparison. Codex CLI ranked first for lowest average cost per task with GLM-5.3 but dropped to 16th out of 22 configurations with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness Creator showed an even larger change, ranking first with Muse before falling to 21st with GLM-5.3 Flash. Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same. Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same. The biggest difference came with DeepSeek, where Cline CLI cost five times as much as OpenCode v1 but delivered a pass rate only two percentage points higher. The researchers also shuffled the trials within each model 300 times to see whether random variation could explain the cost differences. The gaps in the actual results were larger than those in the shuffled trials, with a reported p-value of 0.003. Failed runs eat the budget Failed runs accounted for 52.7% of estimated inference spending, with timeouts adding another 11.8%. Just 35.5% went toward successful runs. Those costs are based on Baseten’s published rates, but they put a price on a familiar problem with coding agents struggling to complete difficult tasks . Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out. Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out. The researchers also found 216 instances of reward hacking in the execution logs, including 163 involving online lookups. All received zero scores. Steps, not prompts, drive cost Runta looked at whether prompt size, tool count, cache hit rates, or agent steps had the biggest impact on cost. Step count was the only factor with a statistically significant correlation to cost per successful task, at 0.51. Mini-SWE-agent showed how multi-step agent execution can drive up token costs , starting with the smallest prompt in the benchmark at 882 tokens but averaging 38 steps per successful task and ranking 17th out of 22 configurations for cost per pass. The five best-value harnesses relied heavily on shell commands, which made up 61% to 93% of their tool calls, and rarely used subagents, or context summarization. Runta didn’t test those design choices separately, however, so the results don’t establish whether the simpler setups were responsible for the lower costs. articles.title: OpenAI Releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol With a 20% Cheaper Astra API
articles.content: OpenAI has released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol , twp closed models aimed at professional and agentic work. The GPT-6.2 Astra model is the new frontier tier for hard, long-horizon tasks. GPT-6.2 Sol is the efficient everyday tier. For developers, the key point is cost per task. Astra’s token prices fall 20%, and OpenAI says both models finish tasks with fewer output tokens. Both are live in the OpenAI API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . TL;DR Size: 1,050,000-token context window, 922,000 max input, 128,000 max output. Runs on: OpenAI’s hosted API, ChatGPT Work and Codex only. Performance: Astra scores 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, second behind Claude Fable 5.2 (65). Best: Astra ranks #1 on AA-3D with 1,318 Elo, ahead of Fable 5.2 (1,271). Worst: Astra posts a 59% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate (Sol: 55%). Sol’s Coding Agent Index drops 3 points. Bottom line: Best: frontier results at much lower cost per task. Worst: no coding gains, and hallucination stays high. What is GPT-6.2 Astra? GPT-6.2 Astra is OpenAI’s frontier reasoning model for complex professional work. It succeeds GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI says it produces cleaner slides, spreadsheets and documents that follow templates and field conventions. It also builds better frontends, games and 3D scenes. GPT-6.2 Sol replaces GPT-6.1 Sol as the everyday model. How do the two models differ? Both accept text and image input and return text. Both share the same context limits . The split is cost and depth. Astra: knowledge cutoff May 18, 2026. Built for the hardest multistep work. Sol: knowledge cutoff June 1, 2026. Built for fast, versatile everyday tasks. Neither model accepts reasoning effort none . OpenAI recommends keeping prompt prefixes unchanged and appending new instructions. That improves cache reuse and preserves reasoning across turns. What do the benchmarks show? OpenAI’s own claims focus on cost-adjusted gains: Agents’ Last Exam v1.1: Astra scores 5.2 points above GPT-6 Astra at under a third of the cost. It leads Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points at 5% of the cost. Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1: Astra gains 9 points over GPT-6 Astra at under a third of the cost. articles.title: iFixit Says Apple's HomeView is Unnecessarily Hard to Repair
articles.content: iFixit today tore down the Apple HomeView to see what's inside, and found that the device takes a step backward in repairability compared to the HomePod . Getting into it resulted in damage to internal components. Strong adhesive holds the HomeView's display in place, and iFixit said it was difficult to remove. There's a mix of Phillips and Torx screws in different sizes securing internal components, necessitating several tools. Speakers take up most of the internal space behind the display, with the logic board located behind them. The logic board has a shield that connects to the back of the aluminum enclosure, turning the entire thing into a heat sink to improve thermal performance. The thermal paste and adhesive attaching the shield to the casing made the logic board difficult to remove. The speakers are held in place with a thick adhesive pad, and attempting to remove one caused it to snap in half. There are multiple cables connecting the display to the speaker base, and iFixit found the components of the wall-mounted and tabletop versions of the HomeView aren't interchangeable. The devices have different internal designs, with the wall-mounted version using a larger logic board and the tabletop model adopting larger speakers and a pivot mount. The HomeView speaker base is designed similarly to a ‌HomePod‌, and iFixit found it easier to take apart. The USB-C port on the base is modular and can be replaced, as can the two passive speakers inside the enclosure. Because of how the HomeView is assembled, it isn't possible to separate the display from the base without going through the display side. iFixit said Apple made several design choices that "made repairs unreasonably and unnecessarily difficult" with little thought for repair options. articles.title: Google now lets Gemini users opt out of AI training while keeping their chat history
articles.content: Credit: Megan Ellis / Android Authority TL;DR The Gemini app is getting new settings that allow you to keep your chat history while opting out of AI training. If history is turned off, your chats will now be saved for around two months. This will be a global update that arrives in the coming weeks. While not always the case, when you use AI, it’s fairly safe to assume that companies are using your data to train their models. It’s the trade-off you often have to be comfortable with if you want to use these products. However, Google is now updating the Gemini app to give users a new option. In a brief blog post , Google announced it is giving you more control over when your Gemini chat history is used for generative AI training. The update will introduce new settings that will let you opt out of training while keeping your chat history. Additionally, you’ll still be able to control how long your history is stored and review or delete history manually.

articles.title: Optimizely Hack Turns World's Biggest Websites Into Malware Dispensers
articles.content: PattonPending writes: As reported by The Register, Zoom, the BBC, CNN, HSBC, and numerous other websites briefly served malware on November 16 after an attacker exploited Optimizely's "Experiments" feature to inject JavaScript into their pages through Optimizely's CDN. The malware replaced cryptocurrency addresses, attempted to steal credit card information and cookies, and sought to compromise iOS devices. Websites belonging to at least 178 organizations were affected via the "OPTIMJACK" vulnerability, which has since been patched. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects," the company said. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." The researchers said they found malicious code in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined, including those on the company's own website and login portal, suggesting the number of affected businesses could be significantly higher. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Apple Blames Internal Update for Outage, Says It Wasn't a Cyberattack
articles.content: Apple has largely resolved outages affecting iCloud accounts, retail stores, and more, the company said in a statement to Bloomberg . Apple said the outages were due to an unspecified "internal update" and were not caused by a cyberattack. The company is working to get remaining systems online "as soon as possible." Issues started around 11:45 a.m. ET, with social media reports suggesting users were unable to access their Apple Accounts or sign in to services. Apple retail store systems were also offline, and customers in stores were not able to complete purchases. The System Status page is still listing issues with ‌iCloud‌ Accounts and Sign In, AppleCare on Device, Apple Business, Apple School Manager, Schoolwork, ‌iCloud‌ Mail, and ‌iCloud‌ Web Apps. Services are listed as slow or unavailable. The Apple outage follows other major outages over the last few days that caused an FAA nationwide ground stop and impacted Microsoft 365 services worldwide. This article, " Apple Blames Internal Update for Outage, Says It Wasn't a Cyberattack " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Google Home app will show estimated Nest Thermostat energy savings next month
articles.content: TL;DR Google is sharing its latest Home upgrades today, including previews of a few upcoming Nest Thermostat features. Remote thermometer support is finally being expanded generally to compatible Matter devices. Users will soon be able to view estimated energy savings in the Google Home app. Google’s announcing a whole lot of smart home news today, and that involves a number of upgrades for Nest Thermostats , including a Dynamic Farsight update, new tools for estimating energy savings, and better sensor support. Let’s start with Dynamic Farsight , which we first saw arrive with the Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen) back in 2024. The idea behind the feature was to give users at-a-glance information like time and temperature that didn’t require you to be right on top of the unit to see it, instead designed to be visible from across a room.

The 256GB model is currently discounted to $649 ( Amazon , Best Buy , Target ), while the 512GB model with Touch ID is down to $749 ( Amazon , Best Buy , Target ). None of the retailers currently list an end date for the discount, which is the biggest price drop we’ve seen since Apple raised the laptop’s MSRP by $100 in July in response to the ongoing RAM crisis . MacBook Neo Where to Buy: $799 $749 at Amazon (512GB) $699 $649 at Best Buy (256GB) $699 $649 at Amazon (256GB) Apple’s budget-friendly MacBook leverages the A18 Pro processor, a chip originally found in the iPhone 16 Pro, to keep costs down. Both the 256GB and 512GB models feature 8GB of memory, and my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto was impressed by the vivid 13-inch screen and speakers, the latter of which are better than those in many cheap (and even midrange) Windows laptops. The Neo isn’t super performant, especially in terms of storage speed and total memory, but it’s great for everyday tasks, casual use, and students. Read our Apple MacBook Neo review .

articles.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
articles.content: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives." Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows. "Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella. AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world . Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software. "Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot." Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. articles.title: Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom
articles.content: The Aarden team with CEO and founder Danan Margason, third from left. (Aarden Photo) Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments. Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals. “But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement. The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners. Related Aarden AI emerges from stealth with $4M to help landowners navigate deals Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses. The new round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months. Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations. One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses. “Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service. Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres , which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id , which offers property insights and mapping tools. Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact. “We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn .
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler

articles.title: Google Vids now lets you create a personal avatar at no cost
articles.content: Credit: Google TL;DR Google is expanding personal avatars to users with personal Google accounts. Personal avatar lets you create a custom AI-generated avatar. Avatars are linked to your account and are restricted to the account holder’s likeness. Back in March, we spotted that Google was working on a feature that would allow you to turn your likeness into a virtual avatar. That feature would eventually be known as Gemini avatar and later rolled out for Google Vids as personal avatar. While the feature was previously behind a paywall, that’s no longer the case. Google initially announced the plan to roll out custom avatars for Workspace users with personal accounts at the beginning of November. However, a day after the announcement, the company decided to delay the rollout. No explanation was given for the pause, and the tech giant did not offer a resume date. Fast forward to today, personal avatars are now available for personal Google accounts for free.
