articles.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
articles.content: No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. Huang out to dry The US Department of Justice made the rare point of commenting on one of the pillars of the Jensen Huang story on Tuesday when it confirmed that it’s investigating Megaspeed, the Singaporean company formerly helmed by Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), the alleged Chinese spy. The DoJ has been checking the company out since 2024, when Alice Huang was still in charge, over potential export control violations. In other words, the DoJ is hinting that even if Alice Huang isn’t a spy, Megaspeed may have still been moving illegal chips. The DoJ added that Nvidia blacklisted Megaspeed in 2025, and that the Department of Commerce previously interviewed Alice Huang around the same time. It was immediately after that, the DoJ said, that it took over the investigation. “The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the DoJ said. In other words, this is far from over and Nvidia might be justified in wanting not to touch its founder with a ten-foot pole. ®

articles.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
articles.content: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock . Why unneeded model calls add up The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost. At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways: Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps. Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds. Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower. Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked. Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens , often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all? How to decide whether a step needs a model Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements: Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first. Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema? Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no? If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model. Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart. # Step Path through the chart Where it runs 1 Check an order number’s format A rule can check success. Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation, or an AWS Lambda function 2 Route a message by intent A rule settles part of it. A keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question. An AWS Step Functions Choice state that uses JSONata. The residual goes to a constrained decision call. 3 Extract a tracking number from a carrier email A model can write the rule once. It drafts a regular expression, and you review and commit it. Code, as a committed pattern in AWS Lambda 4 Pick one of four support queues for a ticket The answer comes from a fixed list. A constrained decision call. Unsure answers escalate to the right-sized model. 5 Draft a reply to the customer The task is open-ended. The right-sized model, the smallest Amazon Bedrock model that meets the requirements You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model. Property Deterministic code Model call Cost per invocation Typically orders of magnitude lower Per-token, non-trivial at scale Latency Single-digit milliseconds or less Hundreds of milliseconds…

articles.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
articles.content: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength . In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints. How KV-aware routing works KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request. When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG , the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match. The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the…

articles.title: 178 Organizations Served Malware Through Optimizely. What Have the Companies Said?
articles.content: An Optimizely vulnerability put malicious code into scripts used by major websites. The public record now includes a direct Zoom security notice, a Salesforce advisory, an Optimizely incident statement and responses from Equifax and IKEA to Reuters. That is evidence of company acknowledgment, not proof that every website visitor was notified. What happened On November 16, attackers used a vulnerability in Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to customer projects. The code was served through legitimate Optimizely snippets on prominent websites. This is not evidence that attackers separately penetrated the networks of all 178 organizations. Report URI primary investigation | Independent BleepingComputer coverage How the malware worked Crypto address substitution The payload changed valid wallet addresses in page content, clipboard interactions and some outgoing requests. Researchers traced roughly $7,040 in receipts to identified wallets by November 16, but the total attributable loss remains uncertain. Card skimming At 13:43 UTC, the attacker added code designed to capture card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs entered into page-accessible forms. Third-party isolated payment iframes were not directly accessible. Browser data The payload could transmit readable cookies and screenshots in connection with address substitutions; HttpOnly cookies were inaccessible. iOS exploitation On certain older iOS versions, the malware attempted to deliver Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. No confirmed number of successful device compromises is publicly established. The response: what companies actually said Optimizely publicly acknowledged that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and added malicious JavaScript to customer projects. The vendor said it fixed the vulnerability and removed injected code. Original vendor notice Zoom also published a direct notice on its Security Bulletins page: it acknowledged the Optimizely incident, said it disabled Optimizely across production environments as a precaution, and said it had not identified an impact on customer data at that time. Primary source: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/ Reuters obtained responses from Equifax (it stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence its own systems were compromised) and IKEA (it was assessing potential impact). These are statements to a reporter, not evidence of visitor notification. Source: https://www.marketscreener.com/news/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-ce785edfde89f625 Separate company-issued public statements remain unverified for most entries. The register below is a source audit, not a count of companies that notified customers; notification totals cannot yet be established. Timeline 04:21 UTC — First observed malicious Optimizely snippet, on BBC. 08:10 — First identified build of the crypto-address clipper. 11:20 — Zoom snippet modification timestamp. 13:43 — Payment-card skimmer added. 17:13–17:57 — iOS exploit-delivery infrastructure expanded. 19:24–19:59 — Report URI scanned and identified widespread infection. 20:40–21:52 — Mass cleanup; only one previously affected snippet still infected at 21:52. November 17 — Optimizely acknowledged the incident; Salesforce issued its advisory. The unanswered questions How did the signup-flow vulnerability confer access across unrelated projects? How many visitors loaded the code? How many cards, cookies and devices were actually compromised? Which organizations notified customers? Why did many affected hosts lack an effective Content Security Policy? Independent evidence and public statements: sources beyond the original inventory Optimizely incident status — Vendor confirmation of exploit, remediation and affected projects. Salesforce Trust advisory — Company-issued statement about Salesforce-branded sites. StepSecurity OPTIMJACK analysis — Independent urlscan captures on 17 named domains, plus 13 additional…

articles.content: TL;DR Google expands Tasks to call businesses on a user’s behalf, schedule appointments, and make purchases. Users can also text and email tasks to Gemini outside the app. Tasks is now free in six countries. Google is turning Tasks in Gemini from a feature that was only for paid subscribers into something that’s free, while also expanding Tasks to let Gemini act as a more independent assistant. Gemini Tasks started life as Gemini Spark back in May and got a name change just last month. With this update today, it can call businesses on a user’s behalf, schedule appointments, and make purchases. It can also do these things outside of the app, with the ability for people to email or text Gemini .

articles.title: Nvidia employee warns of 'irreplaceable' talent exodus if Jensen Huang not reinstated
articles.content: Following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang , there are warnings that important Nvidia employees are planning to leave if the company doesn’t reinstate him. According to the Wall Street Journal , an employee sent an internal letter to the top executives and board of directors stating that “failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’” Huang resigned last week amidst a firestorm of reports about an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang , a further affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell, and allegations the former relationship may have facilitated chip smuggling into China. According to WSJ ’s sources, director of developer technology Nader Khalil wrote the letter, urging that Huang be reinstated as CEO, lest the company lose loyal and important employees. The letter’s recipients, according to WSJ, comprised roughly 60 direct reports and the 10 members of the board, and Khalil warned that “Irreplaceable talent at Nvidia is now contemplating departing.” The internal letter, along with the standwithjensen.com open letter to reinstate him, shows how important Huang is to the employees of Nvidia. Without the key long-term employees, which the company heavily depends on, progress could halt, or possibly regress, as Nvidia would lose the employees who have worked on and built the architectures and systems that make Nvidia what it is, along with their leader, Huang — who has recently stated that he would be honored to come back as CEO . The open letter, signed by multiple Nvidia current and former employees, and tech CEOs and investors, states that employees are concerned that Huang was ousted unfairly and without due process, expressing that the employees do not have “access to the board’s private deliberations,” and that they have not been shown evidence that Alice Huang was indeed a spy, which even US intelligence doesn’t have solid evidence of. The open letter demands that Huang be reinstated as CEO while ensuring an independent investigation and a fair hearing, including providing a “specific, evidence-based explanation” of why Nvidia shouldn’t keep Huang as CEO — with Huang scheduled to appear before a House of Foreign Affairs panel concerning his affairs with the alleged spy. Despite the letter, the support of other Silicon Valley CEOs, and even President Trump , Nvidia is still not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Nvidia is the hottest AI hardware company at the moment, and its employees are highly desirable not only within the US, but possibly China as well. China surely wouldn’t mind getting its hands on a few key employees, who, if they choose to leave, are likely not going to have a hard time finding another job.
articles.author: Jhet Borja

articles.title: 10 desk upgrade gifts to improve PC work and gaming spaces
articles.content: It’s a tough time for PC gamers and enthusiasts. Graphics cards are scarce, RAM and storage are prohibitively expensive, and the PC port of GTA VI isn’t expected until sometime in 2027 at the earliest . But core components aside, there are plenty of other ways to improve someone's PC PC-related experience, and upgrading their desk space is a good place to start looking. We’ve already covered key peripherals, like keyboards and gaming accessories, so below we’ll be focusing on desk devices that let you connect more devices, stay more organized, improve comfort, or just keep things cleaner. From some of the best desk-friendly PC speakers I’ve tested to tactile media and software controls, and a monitor riser that integrates a USB hub and charging, there’s something here to improve everyone’s desk experience. I own most of these devices, or similar previous-gen versions that are no longer available, and can attest to their usefulness. Some live on my desk at the office, while others are better suited for home PC setups, but they all make for a better experience when I'm at my desk. L-Shaped Elbow Pad and Wrist Rest: was $19.99 now $16.98 These unique wrist and elbow rests are designed to hang over the edge of your desk, making them great for those who lean on their elbows, or just for a cramped desk setup. Available in multiple colors and sizes, the 11.8-inch version I have is wide enough that I only need to use one for my compact keyboard at work. So I use the other one at home for my gaming setup. View Deal MagStand Charging Station: $115.99 If your phone has magnetic wireless Qi charging, there's no nicer, more convenient way to charge it than a stand like this, especially when there's additional power and ports for other devices. This Anker model has a built-in retractable cable that can handle up to 60W, so you can charge a non-gaming laptop with this stand at the same time as your phone. I've used a similar charging stand for years, and it helps keep things clean while making charging a second device as simple as grabbing the pull-out cable. View Deal 11-in-1 Hybrid USB Hub: was $49.98 now $42.49 With 11 ports and up to 10 Gbps speed, a solid aluminum shell, and buttons so you can cut power to individual ports, this USB hub is a great addition to a desk without enough ports. It has external power for better stability, and even a 20W USB-C PD port on the end for charging phones or peripherals. View Deal Volume Control Knob + Media Buttons: was $30.39 now $25.83 Just plug this simple device into a USB port, and you can control the volume and select tracks without reaching for your keyboard or mouse. It supports recent Windows versions, as well as Mac, without the need for a driver. View Deal The Stream Deck Mini features six configurable buttons for launching software or controlling devices. It's compatible with the full suite of Stream Deck tools from Elgato. There are cheaper alternatives, but the ecosystem (supporting software as well as lights and smart devices) makes these devices more versatile than the competition. View Deal Headphone Stand with USB Charger: $14.99 This quirky device combines an under-desk headphone hook and a 20W PD USB charger with one USB-C and two USB-A ports. It brings a bit of extra convenience and tidiness to your desk setup. It comes in four colors and I've been using one under my standing desk since 2023. They're a great audio upgrade to most desk setups, and I have a pair that I bought in 2012 that still look and sound as good as they did when they were new. articles.title: Final Cut Pro Now Includes MotionVFX for Creator Studio Users
articles.content: Apple today updated Final Cut Pro (FCP), adding MotionVFX integration. Apple purchased the company earlier this year, so now the MotionVFX library is part of FCP. It includes the templates, titles, themes, effects, layouts, and transitions that are popular with creators. Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos. MotionVFX graphics and effects can be dropped into a video timeline, and 3D titles and graphics can be added to a scene on moving surfaces or at a natural depth that matches camera movement. Masking improvements make it quicker to add outlines, accents, motion trails, and more to video subjects, and static photos and illustrations can be turned into animations. There's a new Content Hub with access to stock video, photos, graphics, and backgrounds. Creators can also generate images in FCP with text descriptions, and then edit those images. Any image from an FCP project can be opened in Pixelmator Pro for editing, and then added back to FCP when editing is finished. Apple added easing options for more precise control over animation, and there's a new timeline command for detaching a clip from the primary storyline to reposition it freely without affecting B-roll, titles, and audio. The new features are included in the Creator Studio version of Final Cut Pro, so you will need a Creator Studio subscription to use them. Creator Studio is priced at $12.99 per month and includes access to Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, Compressor, and special features in free apps like Pages, Keynote, and Numbers. The one-time purchase version of Final Cut Pro does not include the new additions. Update : Apple's outage today has delayed the release of the Final Cut Pro update, but it should be out shortly. articles.title: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained
articles.content: Data retention has become one of the most misunderstood terms in AI infrastructure. After a wave of AI security headlines, many dev teams now ask a simple question. Does my AI provider keep my data? The honest answer depends on how you send it. Send a prompt to an inference API, and it is processed and returned without being kept. That design is called zero data retention (ZDR). Upload a dataset for a batch job, and it stays stored until you delete it. Both are standard designs, and in both the customer is in control. What changes is who manages the data lifecycle, and where. Fireworks AI cofounder and CEO Lin Qiao set out a clear way to think about this. In a November 13, 2026 post on X , she described two standard API designs. Each one decides where control of the data lifecycle sits. The same split has shaped data processing systems for decades. In this article, we will go through that framework with examples from public API documentation. TL;DR The framework: Two standard API designs : upload, use, delete, or send, compute, return. What it is: ZDR is a per-endpoint commitment not to persist covered prompts and outputs after an eligible request. Where it applies: Eligibility depends on the endpoint, request flags and account settings, not the vendor name. Stored features: Batch, file and dataset features keep data until it is deleted or expires. Bottom line: Prefer ephemeral endpoints. If you upload, deletion is your job, so never assume an expiry. What is an AI data retention policy? An AI data retention policy defines what a platform stores from your requests, and for how long. OpenAI’s data controls describe two layers. Application state is data a feature must keep, such as uploaded files. Abuse-monitoring logs are copies held for safety review. A platform can be at zero on one layer and not the other. What are the two common API designs? AI inference and training APIs follow two lifecycle designs. The difference is who manages the data, and where. Pattern 1: Customer-managed retention (upload, use, delete) You create a file or dataset, run jobs against it, then delete it. The platform keeps the data stored and available until you ask for deletion. It cannot know when you are finished unless you define it. So deletion is your job, done through the platform’s APIs. Batch APIs with uploaded datasets are the standard example: OpenAI Batch : upload a JSONL input file, then create the batch. Amazon Bedrock batch inference : input JSONL files sit in an S3 location you choose. Gemini Batch API : jobs run from an input file you provide. Fireworks AI Batch : create a dataset, then submit jobs against it. Once you delete the data, it is gone. According to Fireworks CEO, it keeps nothing after a deletion request . OpenAI non-batch files persist until you delete them. Fireworks AI managed training datasets have no time limit, and the customer deletes them. Amazon Bedrock and Google batch jobs read and write your own cloud storage. OpenAI batch files last 30 days by default, and Anthropic batch data 29 days. Treat expiry as the exception, and confirm it per feature. Pattern 2: Ephemeral processing (send, compute, return) You send data, the platform computes, and the result comes back. No application state stays behind. Your application owns the conversation history, so no platform cleanup step is needed. This is the pattern ZDR applies to. A synchronous response alone does not establish ZDR. Documented examples: OpenAI Chat Completions : store defaults to false. Amazon Bedrock Converse : content is only used to generate the response. Google Gemini text generation : stateless when store is false. Fireworks AI Chat Completions : direct or through Nexus . The schema has no store field. Fireworks AI Training SDK , including Serverless Training : forward_backward sends tokenized batches per call. No dataset is uploaded , and training data is not stored at rest . articles.title: Putting a spotlight on AI, society, and humanity
articles.content: MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education , and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another. For the MIT Human Insight Collaborative (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing (SERC), to help MIT address them. Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units , offering a total of $5.5 million in funding. Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative. “When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we relate to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS). Eroding “creative friction” Building upon this focus, an AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI. On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it. MITHIC faculty co-lead Seth Mnookin , a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.” “When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.” Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its SHASS+ Connectivity Fund , in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT. In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge. The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently featured in The New York Times . “AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the Times . In another project, CMS/W Professor Eric Klopfer and brain and cognitive sciences Professor Pawan Sinha are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition.…

articles.title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
articles.content: As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record. Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet. In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types. How custom metadata works With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema : field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record. The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean. When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT . A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values. If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException . GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. ( COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.) Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes. What custom metadata makes possible Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance. Ownership and operations Fields such as environment ( prod , staging , or dev ), businessUnit , ownerTeam , supportContact , and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource. Security and…

articles.title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario. Solution overview Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials): Snowflake OAuth : Snowflake acts as its own OAuth authorization server. Each user authenticates directly to Snowflake through the Authorization Code grant (3LO). No external identity provider is needed. Three-legged OAuth using a third-party Identity Provider: Users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant. Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) through its External OAuth security integration. Two-legged OAuth pattern using a third-party IdP: A shared service user authenticates through the client_credentials grant of the IdP. No user interaction or consent is required, which is ideal for machine-to-machine workloads. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side. Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for…

articles.title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
articles.content: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement. Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead. The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation. Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done. Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet. A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory. DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy. And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications. In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world , including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.…

articles.title: Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
articles.content: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python. At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space. In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns , Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register . TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers. Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.) To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well. Debugging a thousand cores C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB , but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info. “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using. In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran . Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate. Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago , which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL). “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said. Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python. Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult. “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns said. A view into parallel Python Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol ) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds. To kick off a debugging session , a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions. The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release. articles.title: Sabey Data Centers Enters 10-Year Solar Agreement for 130 GWh of Renewable Energy Annually
articles.content: Austin, Texas, November 17th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--Sabey Data Centers signed a 10-year virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA) with the operating Greasewood solar project in Texas. The agreement represents 43.5 MW of solar capacity capable of generating an estimated 130 GWh annually, or approximately 1.3 TWh over the 10-year term. VPPA investments can help renewable energy developers secure long-term financing for projects that contribute renewable electricity to the utility grid, supporting energy availability for residential and commercial customers. The 130 GWh of estimated annual generation covered by Sabey’s agreement is equivalent to the electricity needed to power approximately 12,500 households each year. Electricity generated by the Greasewood project flows into the grid, where it can serve homes, businesses, and other utility customers. The VPPA provides Sabey with the environmental attributes associated with its contracted share of renewable generation, supporting the company’s broader sustainability strategy. “Our 2029 net-zero goal requires us to think beyond simply buying renewable energy year to year,” said Casey Mason, Director of Energy & Sustainability at Sabey Data Centers. “This agreement is a long-term commitment that supports renewable generation on the grid and moves us meaningfully closer to where we want to be.” The agreement follows progress reported in Sabey’s 2025 Sustainability Report: Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions fell 29.3% from a 2018 baseline. These figures cover emissions from its operations and electricity purchased for its data center infrastructure, calculated using the market-based method that accounts for electricity procurement and associated certificates. The company’s 2029 climate target is to achieve net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions through direct emissions reductions, energy efficiency and qualifying carbon-free electricity procurement. Any residual Scope 1 emissions will be transparently reported and addressed through independently verified carbon credits. Sabey is also testing hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a renewable alternative to petroleum diesel, in backup generators at SDC Austin. The generators provide power during utility outages and run during scheduled testing and maintenance. The pilot addresses another part of the company’s emissions footprint: the fuel used for backup power. By entering a long-term agreement supporting renewable generation, Sabey is taking a proactive approach to its environmental responsibilities beyond its own facilities. The initiative reflects the company's commitment to supporting a more sustainable energy system that serves both businesses and local communities, while addressing the environmental impact of its growing data center portfolio. About Sabey Data Centers Sabey Data Centers is one of the largest privately owned data center developers and operators in the United States, providing reliable, energy-efficient infrastructure for leading technology, financial, and healthcare organizations. Building on Sabey Corporation’s more than 50-year legacy, the company combines operational excellence with a commitment to environmental responsibility and the communities it serves. Through sustainable innovation, responsible resource management, and long-term community engagement, Sabey strives to support the growing digital economy while remaining a good neighbor in every community where it operates. For more information, visit www.sabeydatacenters.com. Contact Head of PR Ira Tatevosyan Sublime Communications ira@sublimecommunications.com This story was published as a press release by Technologywire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

articles.title: Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down
articles.content: "CNN and other outlets are reporting that a classified network at the NSA is down," writes longtime Slashdot reader frdmfghtr. "This follows a week of major outages at Microsoft, the FAA, and JPMorgan Chase." From a report: The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. "We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about." [...] The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. The NSA released a statement addressing the network issues: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures
articles.content: OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra is nearly twice as likely as its predecessor to leave users unaware of problems that prevented it from finishing a coding task, according to the company’s own safety evaluations. Developers building autonomous agents could encounter the same problem, since OpenAI has added a mitigation to Codex that isn’t automatically applied to direct API requests. In its GPT-6.2 system card , published Tuesday alongside the release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, OpenAI reported that Astra failed to disclose a known obstacle in 22.28% of evaluated coding tasks, compared with 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra. An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job. The copmany says both models perform better on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens, but those improvements don’t necessarily make them more reliable at reporting failures. An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job. The New Stack has asked OpenAI whether it plans to extend the Codex mitigation to API developers and how the additional instructions affect the models’ failure-reporting behavior. Inside the blocker deception test OpenAI measured the behavior with an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, which gives models realistic coding assignments before deliberately introducing obstacles that make the requested work impossible to finish as specified. In some runs, the evaluation removes a source file the agent was supposed to modify. In others, it disables a tool needed to build the project. The evaluation then checks whether the model tells the user what happened or leaves the obstacle out of its final response. The caveats Astra leaves out The company acknowledges the regression and says it is still investigating the cause. One possible explanation is that training the models to give shorter answers with fewer caveats may have made them less likely to report problems that prevented them from completing a task. OpenAI cautions that the evaluation was designed to trigger this behavior, so the results don’t necessarily reflect how often Astra misleads users in production. A separate evaluation, Broken Search Tool, identified a similar problem. The model receives questions requiring information retrieval while the necessary search capability is disabled. GPT-6.2 Astra failed to acknowledge the missing requirement or unavailable tool in 23% of cases, compared with 7.58% for GPT-6 Astra and 1% for GPT-6.1 Terra. Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff … but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed. Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff to see what an agent actually did, but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed. If an agent says it finished the job without mentioning a missing dependency or a failed build, that work could make it through review without anyone realizing there’s a problem. It’s another example of the code confidence gap that becomes harder to manage as agents take on more work across a repository. The fix the API misses OpenAI says it developed a prompt-based intervention that substantially reduced the rate of omitted blockers in evaluations of both Astra and Sol. The company incorporated that intervention into the standard Codex developer prompt at launch, but it does not automatically apply the same instructions to direct API requests. Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t. Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t. OpenAI hasn’t shown whether adding similar instructions to a custom harness would produce the same results. The harness can’t take the model’s completion summary at face value…

articles.title: After Black October, OffSec Turns PHPH2Shell and Other New Vulnerabilities Into Hands-On Labs
articles.content: New York City, United States, November 18th, 2026/CyberNewswire/-- OffSec , the world's leading provider of hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications, released more than 80 hands-on labs in the last two weeks of October as Black October crippled government and university websites across Europe. The labs give security teams a safe place to attack and defend the same kinds of flaws making headlines. Fourteen are built on real CVEs disclosed this year. They include a free lab on PHP2Shell , the PHP flaw at the center of the month's disclosure wave. Black October is the name the security community gave to a cluster of critical disclosures in late October. At its center was PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The flaws let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws with help from AI models. Amazon spotted an exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure. CERT-EU told organizations that could not patch right away to isolate internet-facing apps from public networks. CISA urged immediate patching. The same day GitLab patched a maximum-severity flaw that let unauthenticated users run code on its servers. CrowdStrike reported four threat actors running campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands. The pace reflects a larger shift. AI now helps find flaws and turn them into working exploits . An AI agent can compare a vulnerable release against its patched version and see exactly what changed. That shrinks the window defenders have to understand a flaw and act on it. "AI has lowered the skill ceiling for attackers," said Alex "Sickness" Uifalvi, Security Researcher and architect at OffSec. "Going from a patch to a working exploit used to take a skilled team up to a week. An agent can cut that by a big chunk. Defenders need to get their hands on these flaws while they are still in the news. That is why our team builds labs on real CVEs as fast as we can. You learn what an attack looks like by running it and stopping it yourself." OffSec's new labs, listed in its Oct. 19–25 and Oct. 26–Nov. 2 weekly updates, cover both sides of an incident, and include: Offensive Labs built on recent CVEs in Kestra, Hermes WebUI, WordPress 7.0.2, the Algernon web server and a chained Vite and Uptime Kuma exposure. Defensive Labs where learners secure vulnerable versions of Spring, Kestra and Next.js. Incident Investigations modeled on real attack types. These include ransomware that began with a help desk call, an email compromise that rerouted a client payment, a breached SSL VPN appliance and an intrusion at a hydroelectric plant. AI Targets such as an AI-driven tool marketplace with an automated reviewer and agent. OffSec CEO Ning Wang said fast-moving flaws like PHP2Shell are now the norm. "These vulnerabilities are being found by AI agents and that will happen more and more," said CEO Wang. "You need to very quickly understand how a flaw works and how to defend against it. When PHP2Shell hit, we acted instantly to develop a new lab and a blog to begin teaching people how the attack works and how to stop it. Every organization that cares about its business risk needs to be on top of these things. Your red team and your blue team both need to know how to use AI to do their jobs. It's no longer a nice-to-do. It's a must-do." Level 20: Same Game, New Level OffSec is marking 20 years of hands-on training with Level 20 , a year-end offer for individual learners. Learn One is $550 off through Jan. 4, 2027. Security professionals who want to learn AI red teaming can now train for OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer) through Learn One. This is the first time OSAI is part of a Learn One offer. Its AI-300 course covers attacks on AI models, large language models and autonomous agents. A Learn One Subscription Includes: One 200- or 300-level OffSec course such as PEN-200 for the OSCP penetration testing certification or AI-300 for OSAI 365 days of…

articles.title: What Anthropic’s IPO means for IT buyers
articles.content: Anthropic will make its stock market debut Thursday, seeking a valuation of around $1.3 trillion. While the initial public offering (IPO) is set to attract huge interest from investors, there are implications for Anthropic’s enterprise customers too. The IPO will be “a huge inflection point” in terms of transparency around Anthropic’s operations, said Arun Chandrasekaran , distinguished VP analyst at Gartner. “At the same time, it might also force a different engagement from Anthropic as a company, particularly around longer-term contracts, hybrid pricing models, and so on,” he said. Anthropic had more than 11,900 enterprise customers spending $100,000 or more annually as of the end of September, according to its recent S-1 filing , with over 1,900 spending $1 million or more, and around 250 customers spending $10 million or more. Many of its largest customers are not on long term contracts and have the ability to reduce or, in some cases, cease spending at any point, Anthropic said, though a growing number of enterprise customers are signing annual or multi-year agreements with minimum spending commitments. As a publicly traded company, Anthropic will be under greater pressure to show continued revenue growth and improving margins in its quarterly earnings. This could change how it does business with enterprise customers, say analysts. “Enterprise buyers … can expect a stronger push toward committed-spend and multi-year contracts, because investors reward predictable revenue and visible backlog more than usage that can swing from month to month,” said Nick Patience , VP and practice lead for AI Platforms at Futurum Group. Chandrasekaran agreed, noting that one- to three-year contracts are standard for software as a service vendors, and frontier AI labs such as Anthropic may seek to replicate this. Patrick Moorhead , founder and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, also expects a shift towards longer contracts, alongside an emphasis on “larger prepaid volumes and fewer one-off discounts.” This push to secure longer deals and larger spending commitments could hand customers leverage in negotiations, analysts believe. “Right now, Anthropic wants … the committed revenue,” said Brian Hopkins , Forrester vice president and principal analyst, “so we think this is the time to ask for price protection, rollover of unused credits, the right to shift spend to new models as they ship, and decent exit terms.” Patience added that buyers should use the opportunity to “lock in price protection, capacity guarantees and clear terms on model deprecation.” And, Chandrasekaran suggested, to entice customers to longer deals, Anthropic may also offer benefits such as early access to new features, and opportunities to work with its forward-deployed engineers . However, Patience said, buyers shouldn’t overestimate their potential leverage, such as around negotiating lower prices. With demand for its services currently outstripping supply, Anthropic has “little reason” to cut its prices, he said. Competition from the likes of OpenAI and Google — alongside availability of increasingly capable open-weight models — is likely to have a greater effect on pricing than going public, he said. Hopkins, meanwhile, expects changes to Anthropic’s pricing structure rather than to its list prices, with additional payment tiers and increased bundling of agents, coding tools, and enterprise features. What should IT buyers monitor in Anthropic’s quarterly reports? For Hopkins, a key upside to the IPO for customers is transparency. Aside from the company’s recent S-1 filing, most of the information about the company’s finances to date has come from press leaks, he said, and the quarterly reports will provide customers with figures for revenue, margins, customer concentration, and infrastructure commitments. “I’d make those quarterly filings part of vendor risk management, same as for any strategic supplier,” said Hopkins. articles.title: Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own
articles.content: Microsoft’s Jacob Andreou makes the cost case for Copilot. Click to enlarge. (Microsoft Livestream Screenshot) Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor. “Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco. Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said. Related Satya Nadella kicks off Microsoft Ignite with an Outlook outage mea culpa: ‘We have work to do’ The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said. Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude. For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat. The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude. Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects. The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks. The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said. New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry. The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose. Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription. The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. articles.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
articles.content: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face . Google did not respond to The Register 's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255 , a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident , Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One…

articles.title: 2027 Cybersecurity Excellence Awards Launch With Six New AI Security Categories
articles.content: San Francisco, USA, November 17th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--The Cybersecurity Excellence Awards , presented by Cybersecurity Insiders, announced the official launch of its 2027 awards season, inviting cybersecurity companies, innovators, professionals, and teams worldwide to submit their achievements for independent recognition. Submit a nomination: https://cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com/ The 2027 season introduces six new AI security categories: AI Security Posture Management (AI-SPM), AI Red Teaming, MCP Security, Guardian Agents, AI Usage Control, and AI Supply Chain Security. "In 2024, AI security was one award category. For 2027, we have 18 dedicated categories, because securing AI agents with access to business systems is a different challenge from stopping AI-enabled attacks," said Holger Schulze, founder and CEO of Cybersecurity Insiders. "We want to recognize excellence in each, rather than treating AI security as one market." Recognition Across the Cybersecurity Industry The awards cover cybersecurity products and services, companies, industry solutions, and professionals and teams. Categories span emerging fields such as post-quantum cryptography (PQC) alongside established disciplines including network security, Zero Trust, identity, data security, endpoint protection, and cyber resilience. Independent cybersecurity judges evaluate nominations based on leadership, innovation, and impact, comparing achievements against relevant peers. Every approved nomination also enters Community Choice, a separate public vote that does not influence jury results. Outstanding Gold winners may be considered for Best in Class distinctions throughout the year, without requiring another nomination. Nominations and Key Dates The 2027 Nomination Guide explains award categories, judging criteria, entry requirements, and pricing. Nominees can save their work and complete submissions later. Early-bird pricing is available through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, for entries paid by the deadline. Nominations close February 27, 2027. Jury award winners will be announced the week of March 22, ahead of the RSAC Conference, with Community Choice winners announced in July, ahead of Black Hat USA. Submit a nomination: https://cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com/ Read the Nomination Guide: https://cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com/nomination-guide/ About the Cybersecurity Excellence Awards For more than a decade, the Cybersecurity Excellence Awards have recognized excellence, innovation, and leadership across the cybersecurity industry. The program is presented by Cybersecurity Insiders, a research and media platform backed by a community of more than 600,000 cybersecurity professionals worldwide. Contact Marketing Manager Andrea Chilkott Cybersecurity Excellence Awards info@cybersecurity-excellence-awards.com This story was published as a press release by Cybernewswire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program
