articles.title: Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal
articles.content: The Seattle Police Department Arson/Bomb Squad’s Spot robot from Boston Dynamics. (SPD Photo) Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog. The department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD said in a blog post last week . It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily. SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do. Spot can climb stairs and open doors. (SPD Photo) The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition. The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.” It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work. Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time. Nala, a Seattle Police Department K9 that specializes in electronic detection, can sniff out everything from smart phones to hard drives to micro SD cards. (GeekWire File Photo / Kurt Schlosser) Spot appears decidedly less cuddly. Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later. The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot. Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash , then brought the robots back two years later. Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives. And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

articles.title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
articles.content: Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference. In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models. Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change. Prepare data without hand-building pipelines With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want. Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. You describe the task in a short labeling spec, which is validated against your own examples before the full dataset is labeled. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, such as classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score. Human review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Outside subject matter experts can access the review app through the link in the partner app box in SageMaker Studio. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports. Synthetic data generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale. Data quality evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage. Data transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale. You work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice. For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data.…

articles.title: Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost
articles.content: At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Microsoft announced a number of new AI models, including two new coding models . Imaginatively named Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, these new models promise to come very close to models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost. As Microsoft notes, “MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance” for enterprise coding tasks. “It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.” MAI Code 2 benchmarks The promise here is that Code 2 gets to 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are to run right now). The model, Microsoft says, has also been tuned to create “great dashboards and visualizations” and that it “excels at visual coding.” At least for the OpenAI comparison, it’s worth noting that OpenAI today released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with improved performance. That softens Microsoft’s claims a bit, but it’s worth noting that OpenAI, too, notes that at least on Agents’ Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra is now 5.5 points “ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost” (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are right now). Microsoft MAI Code 2 benchmarks. Credit: Microsoft. MAI Code 2 Flash benchmarks As for MAI Code 2 Flash, Microsoft argues that it can match Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna on benchmarks like DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE Atlas at 20% and 65% of the cost, respectively. Microsoft’s bet: specialist models vs. generalists One interesting wrinkle here is that Microsoft specifically tuned these models for the day-to-day coding work of its users. “They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work,” Microsoft writes. The models Microsoft is comparing these models to are generalists. For a while, OpenAI took a similar approach with its Codex models, but it has abandoned this approach in favor of more general models. Microsoft, meanwhile, which doesn’t build those kinds of in-house frontier models, seems to be focused on smaller specialized models that it can run more efficiently. And while they won’t match the frontier models across every benchmark, focusing on these specific tasks makes a lot of sense in this context. Microsoft is taking this even further with models like MAI Work Flash, a model trained to work across Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ products. Microsoft’s MAI 2 Work. Credit: Microsoft. Availability MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are now available in GitHub Copilot, while Code 2 Flash is in limited preview on Microsoft Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo will soon get support as well. The post Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.title: Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
articles.content: AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators. Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds. The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads. None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time. We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built. The problem has three layers Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations. Layer one: A foundation that compounds Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over. Without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each new use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset. Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. New agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild. Layer two: Automating workflows Next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work. The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? When can an exception clear on its own, and when does it need a person? Experienced employees answer these questions from judgment, and that judgment is rarely written down. Sometimes the…

articles.title: Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push
articles.content: Chee Chew, Sounders FC minority owner and new chief product and technology officer. (Sounders FC Photo) Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI. Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday. “His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.” Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment. He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live. Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams. “In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.” Chee Chew, back row at right in sunglasses, among the expanded Sounders FC ownership group at Lumen Field in 2019. (Sounders FC Photo) Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids. The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry . Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others. A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said. The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said. Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said. “I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.” Chee Chew Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help? On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with…

articles.title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
articles.content: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a…

articles.title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students' academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students' test scores before and after the bans. Schools with strict bans -- requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day -- saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard. U.S. students' test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence. The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans. The annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.) "The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a big role in the decline," said Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. "But we think that's mistaken." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Microsoft’s ARM-based Cobalt 200 chips go GA. Why it matters for AI agents.
articles.content: Microsoft is making its Cobalt 200 virtual machines generally available, with CPU improvements aimed at the sandboxes, tools, and code execution that keep AI agents running. At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, the company announced that the VMs, powered by its second-generation Arm-based CPUs, are available in 14 Azure regions, expanding to 23 by the end of the year. Microsoft says they offer up to 50% better performance compared with Cobalt 100. It’s been almost exactly a year since Microsoft first announced Cobalt 200 and about six months since the new VMs went into preview . Microsoft’s benchmarks show up to 1.5 times the performance for AI agent tool execution compared with Cobalt 100, for workloads like searching files, compiling code, and executing tasks in sandboxes . Pat Stemen, Microsoft’s vice president for Azure Cobalt, tells The New Stack that the team spent part of the past year tuning the infrastructure for these operations. The chip’s large caches, memory performance, and physical cores already suited workloads like starting sandboxes, he says. Microsoft then built “a set of benchmarks inside the company for those common operations” and tuned the product against them. Predictable performance or more speed Cobalt 200 lets developers choose between two processor modes. Deterministic mode runs cores at a consistent 3.2 GHz, while opportunistic mode lets them reach 3.6 GHz when power and thermal headroom allow. Microsoft says opportunistic mode can deliver up to 12% more performance, but clock speeds will vary. “Customers love fixed frequency, by the way,” Stemen says. “They love the predictability that comes with that.” Microsoft recommends deterministic mode for distributed data and analytics clusters, where the slowest node can set the pace, and services with tight performance targets. Web and API services, transaction processing, and media workloads may benefit more from the additional speed of opportunistic mode. Developers can select the mode for each VM when they create it or change it later through the Azure portal, command-line tools, or infrastructure templates. “So if you buy four cores from us,” Stemen says, “you can choose all four of them to run flexibly or deterministically.” He adds that the extra performance is typically available until the machine’s cores are heavily loaded. Designing around Azure workloads Cobalt 200 uses 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores , manufactured on TSMC’s 3nm process, while the VMs scale to 128 vCPUs. Each vCPU corresponds to a full physical core, with 3 MB of private L2 cache. The chip also includes 192 MB of system-level cache and 12 channels of DDR5 memory. Stemen says the move from Cobalt 100 involved switching from a cost-optimized Arm core to a performance-optimized design, alongside larger caches and improved memory bandwidth. Every Cobalt 200 VM also includes Azure Boost , which offloads networking and storage processing from the host. Microsoft reports up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS compared with Cobalt 100. “They need remote storage. They need high-performance networking. They need local SSD,” Stemen says of the workloads customers bring to Azure. Stemen says the team breaks Microsoft’s own workloads into smaller components, models their behavior before the hardware exists, and uses those results to make decisions about cache sizes, memory, and even the fans in a server rack. Product teams participate in the earliest planning reviews. “They’re influencing the beginning of the product from when it’s just in PowerPoint,” Stemen says. The Teams media-processing service, for example, reported 1.65 times the performance on Cobalt 200 compared with Cobalt 100. Microsoft says the service saw linear scaling across physical cores and could load vCPUs to 90% utilization while serving…

articles.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
articles.content: AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings. Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it . AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings? GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH , Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on. The process Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked: Find. Codename MDASH , an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found. Filter. An AI triage agent from the GitHub Security Lab , built on tailored Copilot skills, removed duplicates, checked validity, and focused on high-impact bugs, so maintainers never had to review raw scan results. Verify. Researchers from Microsoft FORGE Lab checked every remaining finding by hand. Report privately. Reports reached maintainers through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix. Fix. Maintainers decided what to fix, how to fix it, and when. Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work. The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release. Participating projects Six projects took part, all alumni of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund . Their maintainers agreed to the scan, received every report privately, decided what to fix, and shared what worked: AutoGPT , an AI agent platform Caddy , a web server Express , a web framework for Node.js FastMCP , a framework for building MCP servers ImageMagick , image processing software Netty , a networking framework for Java What we learned These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons. 1. Fixes matter more than findings Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding. The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes. AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later. Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers. Netty maintainer 2. Codename MDASH, with researcher review, gave maintainers high-quality findings with fixes Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy…

articles.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
articles.content: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap. Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period. The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018. The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say. "What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. "The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026." Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions. Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall. The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses. ®

articles.title: Satya Nadella kicks off Microsoft Ignite with an Outlook outage mea culpa: ‘We have work to do’
articles.content: Satya Nadella addressed last week’s global outage before getting to Copilot or any of the Ignite news. (Microsoft Livestream Screenshot) Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week. Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella said the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.” Related Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.” The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage. It was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20. From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here .

articles.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
articles.content: Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices. In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows. Why one integration per client stopped working GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have. At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity. Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is. Designing a protocol for agents on every client The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients. At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent behavior . Unlike the domains that produced the Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol , the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them. You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal. The result of these requirements is the Agent Host Protocol (AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example. Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them.…

articles.title: Google Wallet Available on iPhone, But Without Tap to Pay
articles.content: Google today said it is bringing Google Wallet to iOS in the United States, giving users a way to make payments and manage purchases across Google services. Google Wallet cannot be used for tap-to-pay purchases in retail locations, but it otherwise serves as an alternative to Apple Wallet. It can store payment cards for online checkout with Google Pay, and it syncs with Gmail and other Google apps for features like package tracking and storing tickets and boarding passes. As with Apple Wallet, Google Wallet lets users add loyalty and gym membership cards, so there's no need to use a physical card. Google says users can manage "agentic purchases made across Google," with easy access to order confirmations, receipts, and delivery updates. Apple began allowing NFC contactless payments in third-party apps with iOS 18.1, but it requires a commercial agreement with Apple, so that may be why Google hasn't implemented support. Google could add contactless payments, but it would need to pay Apple's fees. NFC access is available to app developers in Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, the U.K., and the U.S. Tags: Google , Google Wallet This article, " Google Wallet Available on iPhone, But Without Tap to Pay " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
articles.content: California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state's public nuisance and unfair competition laws. The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI's autonomous agents "may just be the tip of the iceberg," said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing." OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that "OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties," the lawsuit said. OpenAI "knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it," Bonta said in a press release . Read full article Comments
articles.author: Jon Brodkin
articles.fingerprint: admitting after california control incidents loss openai sued

articles.title: Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences
articles.content: November 17, 2026 Category: AI Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences Microsoft Source | 8 minutes New integrations connect Salesforce with Microsoft Copilot, Teams and Fabric, helping enterprises turn Salesforce customer insights into action while maintaining existing security and permissions. New two-way Zero Copy integrations between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric enable organizations to securely query and analyze data across both platforms without maintaining duplicate datasets. Accenture is serving as design and implementation partner and pilot customer, deploying the integrations in its own global sales organization. REDMOND, Wash., and SAN FRANCISCO — Nov. 17, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) and Salesforce Inc. (NYSE: CRM) today announced Copilotforce, a new partnership that helps employees get more done in the tools they already use by bringing Salesforce customer context, business processes and actions into Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity experiences. Unveiled at Microsoft Ignite, the partnership introduces new integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric, including Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin available in public preview with 38+ prebuilt sales skills. Together, these capabilities help businesses move faster, reduce manual work and get more value from their existing technology investments — while maintaining the security, governance and permissions they already rely on. Bringing Salesforce workflows together with conversations, meetings and documents in Microsoft 365 means less time spent moving between systems and more time on the work that matters. Salesforce in Copilot connects customer context with the work happening across the business so employees can make more informed decisions and take action without constantly switching applications. Microsoft Work IQ, the intelligence layer powering Copilot, provides relevant context from Teams meetings, Outlook emails and documents across SharePoint and OneDrive. Work IQ and Salesforce help sellers understand not only what’s recorded in CRM, but what’s happening across customer conversations and collaboration — and what needs to happen next. Through authenticated Salesforce MCP access, sellers can securely retrieve customer information and take supported business actions within their existing Salesforce permissions. Salesforce continues to govern access and business actions, while Microsoft applies its existing enterprise compliance controls to communications and documents. Data, context and the apps where sellers work come to life in practical workflows across the sales cycle, including: Grow Revenue . Use the Pipeline Review and Close Planning skills to decide which opportunities deserve attention and build a concrete path to signature. Customer priorities and deal context inform the proposals and business cases sellers develop in Word and PowerPoint, with clear owners, milestones and next steps. Manage Risk. Connect Salesforce opportunity data with customer concerns raised in Outlook, escalations discussed in Teams and unresolved commitments. The Deal Review, Customer Health and Renewal Radar skills see beyond the recorded stage or renewal date to the customer concern in an Outlook thread, the escalation discussed in Teams or the unresolved commitment behind a stalled deal, helping sellers identify where to intervene. Move faster. Turn customer conversations into follow-up drafts, internal recaps and proposed CRM activities using the Call Follow-Up skill. Sellers can review and confirm next steps instead of manually reconstructing conversations and updating multiple systems. With Copilot as the front door to business process, Salesforce in Copilot allows organizations to bring together Salesforce data, workflows, agents and prebuilt skills from the systems they already rely on through Copilot’s open and…

articles.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
articles.content: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people. Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world. The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less. But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable. Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.
articles.author: Casey Crownhart
articles.fingerprint: hit hydropower lows record southwest summer

articles.title: Multiple Apple services were down including Apple Music and iCloud — live updates on sudden outage
articles.content: Multiple Apple services suddenly went down this morning around 9:45 am PT/12:45 pm ET. The outage appears to be affecting iCloud, Apple Support, Apple Pay and the App Store. On Down Detector, we first noticed issues with Apple Pay when outage reports suddenly hit 2,000 in a matter of minutes. Similarly, reports spiked for iCloud, Apple Business Manager and Sign in with Apple. Though different services appear to have varying amounts of reports, suggesting it may not be widespread. Here's what we know so far. November 17, 2026 – 12:53 PM Apple services that appear affected (Image credit: Future) Based on looking at Down Detector here are the services we're seeing affected by the outage: Apple Support Apple Pay iCloud App Store Apple Business Manager Apple Store Apple Music Sign in with Apple Apple card November 17, 2026 – 12:59 PM Most systems Green per Apple On the Apple system status page most every service is listed as available in the green except for iCloud. iCloud Account & Sign In is listed as having an issue. "This service may be slow or unavailable." the page reads. November 17, 2026 – 1:05 PM Apple users and conspiracy theories (Image credit: Shutterstock) There's a megathread over on Reddit tracking downed Apple services and letting people share their experiences. But also if you're of the mindset that all of this has been planned or its an attack you're free to indulge in some conspiracy theorizing. Based on the reporting though, I do think this might be a server-specific issue, and I'm not yet certain which regional servers are affected. The EU seems to be okay. November 17, 2026 – 1:12 PM Developer page tells a worse story (Image credit: Shutterstock) I mentioned the Apple status page in a previous post, but that only showed an incident at the time. There is a separate Developer status page showing even more outages. The page lists multiple instances across different apps, so I'm combining them into one overall app. For example, Apple Music API, Music Connect and Music for Artists are all down, but I'm lumping them under Apple Music for now. Here are the services it shows as suffering from an outage: Accounts App Store Apple Music Apple Podcasts November 17, 2026 – 1:20 PM Some services returning to normal? (Image credit: Apple) While I am seeing outages on Apple's status pages and there are still reports for iCloud and Apple Music it appears some services may be coming back online. articles.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
articles.content: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now , was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader . Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List , a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma , which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices . Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco . The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun. Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS project that is used by nearly half a million non-techie people. For many of Crosspoint Reader's users, it's the first time they have ever used open source. Some want tech support. Many demand features that can't fit into these tiny devices. Even when the requests are modest and feasible, such a large user base means that people want a wide range of functionality – and thanks to inexpensive cloud LLMs, even totally non-technical users can try to add new functions for themselves. The result is multiple code submissions every day. Many might fit on their own, but it's impossible to fit them all in. So many queries and submissions puts considerable stress on the volunteer maintainers. Mitchell mentioned a possibility that they – and we – had never dreamed of: that of pull requests (GitHub parlance for code submissions) from people using such extensive automation that the submitters don’t realize that they’re sending them. One submitter sent 10,000 pull requests in a single month. The…

articles.title: Replit’s agent swarms built an app monitoring platform in 2 days on a $3K budget. Now, it’s offering them to customers.
articles.content: Agent swarms are all the rage, as companies set about finding ways to coordinate multiple AI agents to tackle complex tasks in parallel. In the past week alone, Google and Cursor unveiled competing approaches to multi-agent coding, building on existing efforts from companies including Anthropic, whose experimental Claude Code Agent Teams feature lets multiple agents collaborate on development tasks. OpenAI has also explored shared workspaces for agents . On Tuesday, Replit revealed that it’s tapping deeper into the trend with Missions , a new product that lets users set objectives, establish budgets and approval requirements, and deploy swarms of AI agents to pursue them over hours, days, or even weeks. How Replit Missions works At its core, Missions is a way to delegate complex projects to AI agents, leaving them to determine how best to achieve a specified goal. Users establish the parameters through what Replit calls a Mission Agreement, which sets out success criteria, spending limits and actions requiring human approval. To get started, users can type /mission in a conversation and describe their objective in plain English, such as getting every page on a website to load in under 500 milliseconds. Starting a Mission Crucially, users aren’t expected to devise a detailed plan upfront, giving agents the freedom to determine how best to approach a problem and adapt their methods as work progresses. Replit president Michele Catasta says this is a very deliberate design choice, as requiring users to map out every step in advance could constrain the agents’ ability to find effective solutions. “That would force the human to worry about implementation details, and not afford the flexibility the AI system might need to accomplish complex objectives.” “That would force the human to worry about implementation details, and not afford the flexibility the AI system might need to accomplish complex objectives,” Catasta tells The New Stack . A separate AI agent then evaluates the work against the agreed success criteria, sending it back for revisions if necessary before the user reviews the results. Missions dashboard and setup interface The concept has parallels with other multi-agent tools, including Factory, which launched its own product called Missions earlier this year . Catasta argues that Replit’s approach differs in how it establishes user intent upfront, alongside the controls and infrastructure available to its agents. For example, each agent operates in its own isolated cloud environment, with access to development tools, integrations and infrastructure such as databases, authentication and deployment. Moreover, users must set a spending limit before a mission begins. Replit checks spending against that budget at every step, blocking further use of paid services once the limit is reached. Catasta argues that such controls are particularly important when multiple agents are operating autonomously. “Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs.” “Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs,” Catasta says. Missions accomplished Ahead of the launch, Replit says it used Missions to build Radar, its own application monitoring platform. According to the company, agents developed the system with direction from Replit engineers, completing it in two days with a $3,000 budget and producing dashboards, alerts and application tracing capabilities. Replit then deliberately introduced a database fault to test the system, with Radar identifying the problem and raising an alert in 38 seconds, beating a 60-second target. In a separate three-hour test, the company says, it processed 26 million activity records and 4.4 million log entries without losing data. articles.title: BugMeNot Calls It Quits
articles.content: BugMeNot, the password-sharing service launched in 2003 to help users bypass website registration requirements, has shut down without explanation after more than two decades. All that's left on the website is a farewell message that reads: "Thanks to everyone who envisioned a better internet." heise online reports: Founded by Guy King, the service had been online since 2003: BugMeNot was a collection of login credentials for various online services. Volunteers submitted credentials they had created for different websites. The idea was simple: Nobody wants to create a full account and provide all their sensitive information just to use a service occasionally. Two decades ago, this privacy concern was more firmly embedded in the public consciousness, but it has since faded considerably. Back then, usernames and passwords were usually the only access controls, so people could easily submit those credentials. Multifactor authentication was still exotic, and passkeys were a distant prospect. The once-popular service lost its shine after just a few years. Service providers quickly discovered and blocked most of the credentials. They could also prevent users from saving logins for their services directly through BugMeNot, for example when those services were paid. More modern security mechanisms also emerged in recent years. As a result, credentials found on BugMeNot rarely worked. Most online providers also blocked the service's disposable email addresses under @bugmenot.com, making them rarely usable. Many people forgot about the site. Now its operators have shut it down without giving a reason. Additional discussions about BugMeNot's closure can be found on Reddit and Hacker News. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Nvidia claims its Vera CPU can gain up to 39% performance boost via software optimization at SC26 — architectural fine-tuning is needed to fully unleash custom Olympus cores
articles.content: Nvidia's Vera CPU, designed as both a standalone data-center part and a host for Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 servers, offers impressive performance thanks to substantially higher execution resources per core than its predecessor, Grace. However, Nvidia admits at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) that existing software cannot always take full advantage of Vera's resources without adaptation for the architecture. The company shared that architecture-specific software optimizations can boost Vera's performance by nearly 39% in certain computationally intensive workloads. But despite offering unbeatable single-thread performance, the CPU is not positioned for general-purpose workloads. Get the Tom's Hardware App (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Get the full Tom's Hardware experience on your device with our brand-new app. Bookmark articles, use our smart search feature, personalize your feed, and get push notifications so you never miss a beat. Download now on Apple App Store Download now on the Google Play Store Unlike Grace, which relies on off-the-shelf Neoverse V2 CPU cores developed by Arm, Vera uses Nvidia's proprietary Olympus cores specifically designed to maximize per-core performance as well as to ensure high aggregate throughput. To that end, Nvidia equipped Olympus with a wide front end that features a 10-wide decoder, a neural branch predictor, a deep out-of-order execution engine, six vector execution units, four load pipelines, two store pipelines, all backed with large private caches and advanced prefetch mechanisms. (Image credit: Nvidia) In fact, Nvidia deliberately opted for 88 high-performance general-purpose cores with support for its proprietary spatial multithreading technology (176 threads in total) rather than maximizing the number of cores per socket, as the maximum possible single-thread performance was one of the key design goals for Vera. "CPU design is really just a game of trade-offs," said Hannah Coutand, who leads Vera CPU marketing at Nvidia, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium . "You could maximize for a lot of cores, but literally when you maximize the die for lots of cores, you do not actually have space to maximize for IPC, like instructions per clock." Although Nvidia primarily positions Vera as a CPU for agentic AI and other AI-related workloads, the company originally conceived its Olympus microarchitecture with data processing applications in mind. As it turned out, the key attributes of Vera — high per-core performance, high memory bandwidth, and low memory access latency — are precisely what agentic AI workloads need as well, according to Coutand. "We are very clear in our strategy with Vera and our positioning with Vera that it is not a general-purpose CPU," Coutand said. " If you want a web server for your cloud data center, there are probably other choices that are better suited for that than Vera. [Vera is made for] workloads […] that require that high per-core speed, high memory bandwidth, low latency. […] It has great fungibility for lots of workloads as long as those workloads value the things that Vera is good for." Software optimizations make good things better To assess the computational capabilities of Nvidia's custom Olympus microarchitecture and its advantages over Neoverse V2, Nvidia's researchers used a double-precision general matrix multiplication (DGEMM) workload based on an assembly kernel from OpenBLAS, an open-source linear algebra library. While OpenBLAS features a kernel tailored for the Arm Neoverse V2 cores that power Nvidia's Grace processor, it lacks one specifically designed for Olympus. To examine the efficiency of the two microarchitectures, the researchers used a standalone benchmark called miniKernelGEMM with a 128 × 128 matrix multiplication problem that fits into the L1 cache of both processors. articles.title: Inside Hank Green’s plan to protect kids (and their parents) from YouTube
articles.content: Pity the parent trying to pull the plug on YouTube, Netflix, or Disney Plus mid-video. The tears! The world-ending wails! Hank Green, host of popular YouTube channels Crash Course and SciShow , has been that parent. A longtime science educator and the co-creator of VidCon , Green has fought his fair share of “turn it off” battles with his son. “These systems are designed to keep kids watching,” he says of advertising-based platforms like YouTube and TikTok . “They don’t have any incentives to even consider designing a ‘stop’ experience.” But parents, on the other hand, are highly incentivized to seek out an alternative to the endless scroll of sometimes questionable content that streams to family devices. Green hopes they will give his new venture, ClockwiseTV, a chance. Launching publicly today, ClockwiseTV is a subscription-based app featuring curated creator videos for kids ages 8-12. Parents establish a session length when opening the app; once kids start watching, ClockwiseTV helps them pick a video sequence that concludes when their session concludes. The app’s constrained choice philosophy extends to the video selection experience. Instead of infinite options, ClockwiseTV presents kids with a menu of just a dozen videos at a time, based on their interests (animals, space, history, etc). Each video has been vetted by a human and scrubbed of any inappropriate language. Creators in the initial library include Animal Wonders Montana, NerdForge, Crash Course Kids, and MinuteEarth. At launch, a subscription costs $6.99 a month or $69.99 a year. There are no ads, and the app is compliant with the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA. [Image: ClockwiseTV] No autoplay, no rabbit holes ClockwiseTV joins a growing array of products designed to keep kids entertained without algorithms or ads. For screen-free audio content, there are Yoto players and Tonie boxes. For kids who want to gab with their besties, there is the Tin Can phone, which mimics the experience of a landline for an approved set of friends and family. There are even sticker printers that use AI to turn kids’ ideas into black-and-white stickers they can color and decorate. Hank Green [Photo: ClockwiseTV] Green says he’s been working on ClockwiseTV for about a year. The decision to focus on tweens stems from his own experience as a parent. “My son is this age, so that’s part of it,” he says. “There’s a kind of no-man’s-land of content where it’s like, you’re done with Mr. Rogers, here’s all of YouTube. I think that’s probably not the right way to do it.” Over time, he adds, ClockwiseTV may pursue “other slices of the pie” and expand its target audience. Leslie Morgan [Photo: ClockwiseTV] More than half of children own a smartphone by age 11, according to Common Sense Media’s 2026 census. The average tween spends five hours a day watching entertainment on a screen, the census found. Leslie Morgan, who has worked in digital media with creators for more than a decade, joined ClockwiseTV as CEO in January. Like Green, she hopes to help parents avoid the internet’s darker corners. “There are no rabbit holes, there’s no autoplay,” Morgan says of the app. Incentivizing kid-friendly creators ClockwiseTV is paying creators to license their content. “A lot of these creators would love to get in front of a younger audience, and it’s not financially viable,” says Morgan, explaining that labeling content as “made for kids” on YouTube typically lowers creators’ AdSense revenue. “For them, it doesn’t make economic sense.” With ClockwiseTV, she argues, creators can access new audiences and supplement their income from other platforms. When I watch YouTube with my kids, it’s often a stressful experience. Typically they’ve requested to revisit a favorite video that, in their view, is very specific (“the tap dancing man in the hat!”). It’s up to me to weed through a confounding list of thumbnails and keyword-optimized titles, searching for an elusive winner, while they…

articles.title: People’s AI secrets raise questions about the use of chatbots in personal life
articles.content: A purple box set up on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square could have been mistaken for a tissue box. Instead, it held dozens of secrets. Olivia Tai was nearby, watching as passersby puzzled over a sign that read, “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret.” Among confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages : “I had AI write my breakup text.” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text.” “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.” “I used AI to win an argument. Lol, not proud, but I won.” Tai, an artist who has repeated the project more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, said calling it a “confession” suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty. But they used it anyway. As more people turn to a chatbot to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using it for personal messages cross a line? Is it ever OK to use AI to write a holiday card or birthday message? What about a love letter or wedding vows? Some use AI to write personal messages, even if they feel guilty about it As part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, Danielle Hass conducted vignette-based experiments to determine how people felt about using AI to write personal messages. She found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who hadn’t. “Everyone felt guilty,” said Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia. “The driver of this relationship was dishonesty, that people felt like they were manipulating.” Even if people are honest about their AI use, others still view them negatively, said Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK. Claessens says his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy. He noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes. But something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off, he said. “What we really want in our social relationships is for people to put effort in, because it shows that as a signal that you’re invested in the relationship,” he said. How to know when it’s not OK to use AI Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it’s appropriate and when it’s not. She suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide. If you imagine using AI to write your wedding vows, would you be comfortable telling your partner you used it? If not, then don’t. “Personal messages don’t need to be perfect,” Newman said. “Part of what makes these messages authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect.” Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who doesn’t share a native language. People with learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, could also use it for help. Hass believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she’s glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages. “Guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings,” Hass said. “It’s showing us, ‘hey, this is where you’re supposed to be human.'” Albert Stumm writes about travel, food and wellness. Find his work at https://www.albertstumm.com —Albert Stumm, Associated Press

articles.title: SAP's cloud migration chief is migrating to Ionos as CEO
articles.content: SAP chief customer officer Thomas Saueressig is leaving the German software giant to become CEO of hosting and cloud provider Ionos. The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1. In January, Saueressig will begin handing over responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, currently a regional customer success president, who will take charge on an interim basis. SAP's supervisory board is searching for a permanent successor. Saueressig joined SAP's executive board in 2019 and became chief customer officer in April 2026. He leads the Customer Value Group and is charged with overseeing sales, customer success, services, and delivery, including adoption of SAP's cloud and AI products. In previous roles at SAP, Saueressig was responsible for customer services and delivery. He has also led product engineering, and has served as SAP's in-house CIO responsible for IT strategy and cloud transformation. He joined SAP in 2004 through its combined work-and-study program. His departure follows several changes at the top of SAP in recent years. In September 2024, CTO Jürgen Müller left by mutual agreement following an "incident" at a company event earlier in the year. In a statement, Müller said his behavior had been inappropriate. The company announced he would get paid €7.1 million following his departure. Chief revenue officer Scott Russell also left in 2024 by mutual agreement with the supervisory board. Julia White left the role of chief marketing and solutions officer in August 2024. "Thomas Saueressig has been a valued member of the Executive Board and has made significant contributions to SAP's transformation," said Pekka Ala-Pietilä, chair of SAP's supervisory board. "Over many years, he has helped sharpen SAP's focus on execution, customer value and operational excellence. We thank him for his commitment and wish him all the best for the future." Saueressig's departure comes as SAP pushes to move the ERP systems underpinning thousands of customers' businesses into the cloud – an effort whose operations and infrastructure he helped oversee. ®

The mythological encounters are another major draw, giving the film plenty of visual spectacle. It's a fresh take on one of the most famous stories ever told. As their troubled marriage unravels, arguments and accusations spill beyond the courtroom, with cell phone recordings and social media turning their divorce into a viral public spectacle. The series examines how competing versions of events shape public perception, with tragic consequences. Why you should watch it: This series could be a particularly compelling watch if you enjoy true crime stories that leave you questioning what really happened. The shocking case, conflicting accounts and viral social media footage all add to the intrigue, making it difficult to know who to believe. The documentary's exploration of public opinion is particularly interesting, especially how quickly people can form strong conclusions when they're only seeing fragments of the truth.
