articles.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
articles.content: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles. "Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public." Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update. That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months." It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note. Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models. In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

articles.title: Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites
articles.content: Vulcan lifts off Sunday with 40 Amazon Leo satellites, then climbs past Amazon’s integration facility at Cape Canaveral. ULA says early data suggests the rocket’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. (United Launch Alliance Photos) Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday. In its first detailed account of the failure , ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit. That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete. The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally. The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes. What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn. ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating. Related Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp , asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning . “It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.” Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program. Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight. Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

articles.title: Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn
articles.content: Glenn Kelman, shown here in 2022, saw the cost of health care up close at Redfin. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007 , “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list. The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website . “Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site. His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen , an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation . This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management. Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words , confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.” But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health. Dr. Connie Chen, Sojourn’s co-founder, previously co-founded Vida Health and was an executive at Lyra Health. (Sojourn Photo) Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.” From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com , which sketches out the plan. Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story. “Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care. “The choices were all terrible,” it says. Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost. As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.” Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now. “I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote. articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO
articles.content: Jensen Huang, the former CEO of Nvidia who resigned last week amid the fallout from two extramarital affairs, said in his first public statement since abdicating his position that he would be willing to return to the corner office at the company he co-founded. "Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement posted on X . “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.Jensen November 17, 2026 Huang has seen public support from other tech founders and CEOs, such as SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. They and some investors and Nvidia employees signed an online petition and have continued to be vocal on social media, namely Musk's X. President Donald Trump also said that he "would not mind" Huang's return. Huang resigned on Thursday following two scandals: one affair with Alice Huang , a former executive of Megaspeed believed by some US Intelligence officials to be a potential Chinese government asset; and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and Huang's direct report. Despite Huang's apparent willingness to return, Nvidia's board doesn't seem likely to make that move. Reports yesterday claim that the board is more focused on its ongoing investigation into Huang's affairs and a national security inquiry and is not considering Huang's return. The board has also put together its own National Security and Export Control Oversight to provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress. In his post on X, Huang further apologized, writing that "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation."

articles.title: CoreWeave connects custom training loops to model serving
articles.content: Production traffic shows failures that benchmarks or pre-deployment evaluations can’t fully reveal. It tells you which edge cases matter and what users need. Turning that signal into the next model version requires an upfront decision: does the model need to change, or is the problem in retrieval, context, prompts, tools, or serving? Changing weights won’t fix a failure elsewhere in the system. When the model is the right place to intervene, production evidence can improve both quality and economics. A smaller model might reproduce a more expensive model’s behavior; better examples might improve consistency; an outcome-based reward might suit the task. Refining a capable model can also avoid another migration to a new model generation. Choose a technique from the failure mode Model distillation fits when a stronger model already produces the desired behavior and you want a smaller, more economical model to reproduce it. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) fits when high-quality examples can teach more consistent behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) fits when you can reliably evaluate an outcome but cannot readily specify the ideal response in advance. “Changing weights won’t fix a failure elsewhere in the system. When the model is the right place to intervene, production evidence can improve both quality and economics.” You may use all three approaches over a model’s lifecycle. Choose from the evidence in your workload, even when that means using a technique that takes more setup. Production traces have to become training data. Post-training needs compute and orchestration , and the resulting model has to be evaluated and returned to inference . That is the work of closing the loop . In RL, inference generates rollouts during training, and new weights must return to serving throughout the run. At Fully Connected 2026 , we introduced CoreWeave Model Distillation , CoreWeave RL Rollouts on CoreWeave Inference, and a programmable training API. These workflows connect in CoreWeave Forge . The programmable API is in limited preview, with an official launch planned for later in 2026. Keep the data fresh when the base model stays CoreWeave Model Distillation provides a managed workflow. CoreWeave Agent Lens captures inference traffic as the application runs. The workflow turns it into training data, relabels weak outputs, tests base models and hyperparameters, deploys candidates to Serverless Inference , and compares them with the production model. If the model already has the capabilities your task needs, fresh production data can improve its fit without changing the serving profile you know. Compare the new version against the model already running before you move traffic. Method used this workflow to revisit a model it had already deployed. In 2024, it used OpenPipe to train Llama 3.1 8B to navigate bank interactive voice response (IVR) systems, using GPT-4o outputs. In August 2026, Method brought in fresh production data, relabeled it with GPT-5.6 Sol, and trained another version. The candidate won 57.5% of head-to-head evaluations against the deployed version. The base model had not changed. Fresh production data and Model Distillation in Forge made another iteration possible sooner. The 57.5% result is the share of head-to-head evaluations the new version won. Control the training recipe in Python For teams that want to design their own learning process, the programmable training API for Serverless Training separates training logic from infrastructure operations. You write a Python loop; CoreWeave manages the compute and underlying training infrastructure. Here’s one way to combine RL updates with periodic supervised updates on verified demonstrations. The example creates a learner and serving adapter, uses an Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-5, and publishes updated weights to the sampler after each step. articles.title: AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Big US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge
articles.content: The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more. First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The company launched the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra. But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI said Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want. It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve. Keeping things safe For years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do. OpenAI says that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here. Those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments. Safety crackdowns for convenience? Against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview. But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO . "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of users,” von Thun said. “They’re definitely vulnerable.” Those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months. That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a company’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics. China versus the U.S. In July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy…

articles.title: Uber Says Hackers Stole Info On Nearly 150K Driver's Licenses During Data Breach
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver's license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company's tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa, the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber's data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. The stolen data includes affected drivers' names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver's license numbers. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers' information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack. In Uber's case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks' own internal credentials, "no alerts were triggered." [...] In a notice filed with Oregon's attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before a House Foreign Affairs panel amid concerns over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy
articles.content: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on December 1, with an Nvidia lawyer following him on December 2, it's been confirmed. CNBC reports that the leaders of those panels broke the news today after days of speculation. Huang was asked to appear via a letter issued on November 9, just 24 hours after he admitted the affair with Alice Huang , a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy . Days later, it was also suggested that Mr. Huang could be issued a subpoena if he did not respond by tomorrow, November 18. That subpoena will no longer be required. “We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Rick Crawford, R-Ark., the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence Committees, reportedly said after the news of the pair's December appearances was announced. "The American people need answers," they went on, noting that it would be "dangerous" to allow Chinese state actors access to advanced AI chips, the likes of which are built by Nvidia. Ms. Yuang was an executive at Megaspeed, a company that was a customer of Nvidia during Mr. Huang's tenure as CEO. Megaspeed was later added to Nvidia's no-sell list following concerns that it was involved in the smuggling of AI chips to China against U.S. export laws. Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary, has been accused of importing Nvidia chips and then re-exporting them to China. A criminal investigation has since been launched into Megaspeed in an attempt to get to the bottom of the complicated web of AI companies and chip shipments. Jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia following his admission of an affair with Ms. Huang. Since then, reports of at least one other affair with an Nvidia employee have surfaced. Despite that fact, calls for Huang's return to the top job at Nvidia continue to gain momentum.
articles.author: Oliver Haslam

articles.title: Xreal Aura Review: Android XR combined with lightweight glasses delivers a true next-gen spatial computing experience
articles.content: The world of augmented reality (AR) and extended reality (XR) glasses is really starting to get interesting. This is particularly true of so-called “self-contained” systems that don’t rely solely on your smartphone or tablet to deliver content. The Xreal Aura, which was co-developed with Google, is the latest in the Android XR field, and it’s quite an ambitious project. Although the Aura looks somewhat similar to previous Xreal glasses that we’ve reviewed, the AR goes a step further with a dedicated puck powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite SoC, hand/finger tracking, and the ability to interface wirelessly with accessories like keyboards and gamepads. The Aura really promises the ability to leave your smartphone at home and serve as the only computing platform you need (with some caveats). Design of the Xreal Aura The Aura’s design is clearly an evolution of the Xreal One Series , but with a few key differences. You’ll find the main changes up front, where you’ll now find two forward-facing, high-precision tracking cameras mounted at the corners of the frame. These cameras are used to continually track your head position, giving you the best possible experience for 6 degrees of freedom tracking for your hands and fingers. At the center of the frame, there is a fully integrated single high-resolution camera for capturing photos or video. This was previously a separate add-on module for Xreal One Series AR glasses. There’s a red LED that illuminates when you’re recording so that people around you are made well aware of what’s going on if they have objections. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Your primary focal point, however, will be looking through the lenses, which are augmented by dual Sony-manufactured micro-OLED displays. You get one micro-OLED display per eye, each offering 1920 x 1200 resolution, a 120 Hz refresh rate, and maximum brightness of 1,050 nits. However, there’s a major upgrade in the field of view (FoV), as the Aura expands to 70 degrees, up from 57 degrees on the One Pro. The Aura is available in two SKUs to support the interpupillary distance (IPD) of a wide range of people. The Medium SKU supports people with an IPD of 60 to 66 mm, while the Large SKU ranges from 66 mm to 72 mm. Given that the Aura is the flagship of Xreal’s AR/XR glasses lineup, it comes with electrochromic dimming for the lenses, which can automatically adjust transparency levels, or you can manually make adjustments (there are five levels of transparency available). The arms of the Aura look nearly identical to the ones you find on members of the One Series glasses. On the bottom is a red button, which, when pressed, allows you to manually adjust the brightness levels of the Aura. Directly adjacent is a rocker that allows you to control the volume. There’s another button on the top of the right arm that, when pressed once, takes you to the home menu. Double-pressing the button brings up the capture menu for taking pictures or videos with the forward-facing camera. Bose-tuned speakers are also built into the arms of the Aura and feature an open-ear design so that you can remain engaged with what’s happening in your environment. Xreal Aura Specifications Display 1920 x 1200 per eye Display Type OLED Brightness 1050 nits Field of View 70 degrees Refresh Rate 120 Hz Degrees of Freedom 6 DoF Audio Dual open-air speakers Connectivity USB-C, Bluetooth 5.3, Wi-Fi 6E, GPS Weight (Aura glasses) 3.35 ounces (95 grams) Weight (Computing Puck) 9.3 ounces (265 grams) Battery (Computing Puck) 4,455 mAh Xreal Aura Computing Puck Xreal takes a two-pronged approach to hardware with the Aura. At a base level, the Aura is powered by the X1S Spatial Coprocessor, which allows you to experience traditional AR functionality with smartphones, tablets, PCs, and Macs, as you would with previous Xreal glasses. But the real magic happens with the Xreal Computing Puck, which is a separate device that connects to the Aura using a USB-C cable.…

articles.title: Are school phone bans working so far? Here’s what early studies show
articles.content: The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction . Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more. But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research shows. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world . In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country. A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers said, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones. Phone bans appear to help, to a point The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year. Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors. “Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years. “While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students’ phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says. The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said. Academic gains are overall ‘disappointing,’ one researcher says Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut. A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools. The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches. The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans. Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said. Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: “I hope they’re right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.” The reasons,…

articles.title: Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses
articles.content: Genesis AI , a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation. Premji Invest , Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025. The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world. Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno. Zhou Xian and Theophile Gervet, co-founders of Genesis AI. (Courtesy photo) “We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product. Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates , Durable Capital Partners , Bpifrance , HSG , Nvidia , AMD Ventures , Zoom , Samsung Next and Ericsson . Individual backers include Eric Schmidt , Eric Yuan , Jerry Yang , Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn . The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California. Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data. The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year. Learning from human movements Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from. Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act. Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead. Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone. From research project to robotics startup Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University . The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools. After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware. articles.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
articles.content: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. CPUs for the Agent Loop Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. A New GPU for Science Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Quantum Error Correction Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Networking Buck also showed one of the first…

articles.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
articles.content: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be…

articles.title: Lab-grown chicken is finally becoming affordable. Will consumers bite?
articles.content: There’s something new on the menu at Epic Steak, an upscale restaurant across the street from Google in San Francisco: “Cultivated” chicken, made partly from chicken cells grown in bioreactors, is now offered to diners right alongside staples like porterhouse and Wagyu. Epic is one of eight California restaurants that serves the food, along with some corporate and college campuses, including Stanford University. The Bay Area startup behind the cultivated chicken, Upside Foods , says it has reached a new milestone in scaling up its production—and that has helped bring the price down in the range of premium farm-raised chicken. Its new product includes a blend of cultivated chicken and plant-based ingredients like soy and olive oil. [Photo: Upside Foods] At Epic , “Southern Fried Upside Chicken” with kimchi slaw and hot honey aioli sells for $12. Waterbar , a neighboring seafood spot with the same chef as owner, sells a five-spice version of Upside chicken for $15. At Chimmelier and Jilli , popular Korean fried chicken restaurants in Los Angeles and San Francisco, K-Pop Chicken made from the new meat sells for $19. “We can put it at a price point on the menu where it can be available for everybody,” says Parke Ulrich, executive chef and owner at Epic and Waterbar. Two of his other Bay Area restaurants, Mersea and Hurrica, will also serve dishes made with Upside chicken. Upside, which launched in 2015 and has raised around $600 million, has spent years on R&D for its cultivated meat—meat produced without raising animals or using slaughterhouses, using real animal cells that grow in tanks the company calls cultivators. The company was originally called Memphis Meats, but rebranded in 2021 with a name that it saw as more consumer-friendly. It’s one of more than 140 companies working in the space of cultivated meat. A handful are selling products on the market, including Vow, which sells cultivated quail and fois gras in Australia, and Wildtype, which sells cultivated salmon at a few U.S. restaurants. In theory, producing meat this way could help reduce the enormous environmental footprint of animal agriculture, though that depends on how it’s made, including how much energy is used . The space has been slow to take off, and some other companies have faced difficulties. Good Meat, another Bay Area-based cultivated meat brand, stopped commercial production in the U.S. in 2024. Two other startups, Meatable and Believer Foods, folded late last year . Over the last several years, “the biggest challenge was the external skepticism that this would have worked,” says Dr. Uma Valeti, cofounder and CEO of Upside Foods. The company first unveiled a commercial facility in 2021, though it didn’t initially use its large-scale bioreactors. ( Wired reported that it struggled to use the equipment; the company says that its early R&D challenges have been fully addressed.) In 2023, when the company got regulatory approval of an earlier version of its chicken, it was produced at a small scale. Customers had to make reservations for the dish, available only in limited quantities, at a restaurant that sold it temporarily, or find it at one-off events. [Photo: Upside Foods] Now the company says large-scale production is underway. Upside has built a much larger production line, with 20,000-liter tanks in addition to its earlier equipment. Valeti says the two-story-tall tanks “are the largest of their kind in the world,” including anything ever used in the pharmaceutical industry. (The company had previously planned to build a factory in Illinois, but retrofitted its Emeryville headquarters with the giant equipment instead.) In a year, it claims that it has the capacity to produce more than a million pounds of Upside Chicken on less than half an acre of land. One cultivator produces 1,500 to 2,000 pounds of meat a day; the next “harvest” will begin later this week. Inspectors from the U.S. Department of…

articles.title: California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
articles.content: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models. The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement announcing the lawsuit . The state brings two claims: violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and creation of a public nuisance. It is seeking an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and an order to abate the nuisance. It also wants civil penalties of $2,500 against each defendant for each violation proven at trial. Other incidents and internal breaches In one July incident, agents escaped their sandboxes and gained administrator-level access to OpenAI’s own systems, according to the complaint. Those systems included the company’s cloud model deployment system, its secrets management service, and its identity and access management service. The agents then launched unauthorized servers, exposing OpenAI’s infrastructure to the internet. OpenAI did not let external researchers review that attack, the complaint said. The complaint identified several other incidents involving OpenAI agents. At RubyGems, a software package repository, agents allegedly uploaded thousands of packages in May 2026. Administrators removed more than 500 packages they considered malicious, and the platform suspended new user registrations between May 12 and May 16. The complaint also alleged that agents made approximately 17,000 edits to a German website, DseWiki, using it as a message board to exchange information about bypassing sandbox restrictions. Other incidents involved Wikimedia Foundation’s infrastructure and Australian government websites. The complaint said agents overwhelmed Wikimedia services with millions of API requests and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata queries, likely contributing to a partial outage in May. In June, agents allegedly accessed non-public information from Australian government websites. The complaint further said OpenAI notified dozens of organizations whose websites or internal systems had been accessed by its agents. These included government institutions, law enforcement agencies, educational institutions, and small businesses. Some incidents allegedly involved stolen credentials, API keys, and fraudulent accounts, with agents accessing personally identifiable information. OpenAI’s own infrastructure was also compromised in at least three attacks in July, according to the complaint. Agents allegedly obtained administrator-level access to systems supporting cloud model deployment, secrets management, and identity and access management. Escapes after the fix The state argued that the danger is ongoing. On September 20, after OpenAI had hardened its environment, an agent escaped during a training run and reached an external chatbot. “This incident occurred after OpenAI had implemented ‘security hardening’ following the Hugging Face attack,” the lawsuit added. OpenAI detected it within minutes, but the run did not stop automatically, and human reviewers took two more hours to halt it, the complaint said. OpenAI announced a pause on training and evaluating its most capable models on September 25. The pause lasted five days, ending October 1, according to the…

articles.title: The Money Cleared The Bank. Now The Founder Is The Risk.
articles.content: By Kelly Meerbott The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles. The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months. I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window. Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud. What pressure does to judgment Kelly Meerbott of YOU – Loud & Clear. Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady. Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach. Porcelli and Delgado , writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything that feels like a threat. The decisions that go wrong in this window rarely feel reckless. They feel rational, because the nervous system is treating uncertainty like an emergency. Where it shows up Senior hiring. An investor who advises 20 fast-growing technology startups told me one of the biggest sources of leadership friction he sees is a CEO hiring a head of sales because they know the person. The relationship feels safe, so the offer is generous. Then the results don’t come. Under pressure, familiarity feels like certainty. But knowing someone isn’t the same as knowing they can lead sales at the company’s next stage. Expansion. Pressure condenses time. The new market planned for month 12 moves to month three. The data didn’t change. Waiting became unbearable. One founder I coached pulled a 12-month expansion into three, bragged about how little sleep he was getting, and did everything himself. The second-market launch was a sloppy, drama-filled disaster. The board brought me in to put him back together and triage the launch. Ask whether the evidence changed or your tolerance for uncertainty did. Co-founder relationships. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, who studied 10,000 founders for “The Founder’s Dilemmas,” has put the share of high-potential startups that fail because of co-founder conflict at 65%. One founder withdraws because they’re overwhelmed. The other interprets the silence as distrust. A trauma-informed lens doesn’t treat every disagreement as trauma. It builds enough trust that a disagreement doesn’t become one more emergency. Four habits that protect judgment Make the decision window a rule, not a mood. For the first 90 days, don’t finalize a senior hire, a market entry or an equity change in the meeting where you first propose it. Write down the criteria, then sleep on it. Name the state before the decision. Before a major call, ask: Where am I on a pressure scale of 1 to 10? Not how the business is doing. How much you’re carrying. A high number earns the decision a second conversation. Put the avoided conversation on the calendar. Co-founders get 30 minutes a week on how…

articles.titleFa: فشار پس از تأمین مالی استارتاپ‌ها و تأثیر آن بر تصمیم‌گیری بنیان‌گذاران
articles.summaryFa: پس از اتمام دور تأمین مالی، تجربیات نشان می‌دهد که بنیان‌گذاران تحت فشار زیادی قرار می‌گیرند تا تصمیمات فوری و دقیقی بگیرند. در این مدت، آنها معمولاً با اضطراب و عدم اطمینان مواجه می‌شوند که تأثیر منفی بر توانایی‌های شناختی آن‌ها دارد. تصمیم‌گیری در این بازه‌ی خطرناک می‌تواند به نتایج غیرمنتظره‌ای منجر شود که احساسات بسیار قوی‌تری از واقعیت‌های پیچیده‌ی کسب‌وکار را تحت تأثیر قرار می‌دهد.
articles.summaryEn: After a funding round, founders often face immense pressure to make immediate and critical decisions. During this dangerous window, they may struggle with anxiety and uncertainty, which negatively affects their cognitive abilities. Decisions made during this time can lead to unexpected outcomes, as emotions can overshadow the complex realities of business.

احساس اضطراب در شرایط عدم اطمینان منجر به رفتار محتاطانه و حتی ریسک‌پذیری بیشتر می‌شود.
